articles.title: Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT): Architectural Identification of a Closed Explanatory System
articles.authors: Cara Tonucci
articles.abstract:
This pre-print introduces Dimensional Human Field Theory (DHFT), a foundational explanatory system describing invariant, non-moral, non-psychological mechanics governing human systems across load, detection, identity, power, and time. DHFT is not an application framework and not a theory-in-progress; it is a closed architectural identification of mechanics already governing behavior across individual, institutional, and civic scales.

The system is organized around two co-foundational, non-reducible spines: Dimensional Human Physics (DHP), which defines lawful mechanics of load, constraint, accumulation, movement, and time; and Dimensional Self Architecture (DSA), which models structural identity continuity and stabilization over time. A canon-locked bridge domain, Identity Harmonics, governs lawful coupling between these spines without collapse. A pre-foundational condition domain specifies when mechanics apply at all, prior to cognition or interpretation.

DHFT explicitly refuses moral, psychological, intent-based, therapeutic, or regulatory framing. It distinguishes detection from cognition, authorization from authority, and structural admissibility from consent. Non-collapse constraints prevent interpretive, applicative, or narrative backflow into mechanics.

Dimensional Human Physics (DHP) defines the lawful structural mechanics of load, capacity, and boundary conditions. Despite its name, “physics” refers to structural mechanics rather than material or biological processes. Dimensional Self Architecture (DSA) defines structural identity persistence and operates as a co-equal, non-reducible domain alongside Dimensional Human Physics (DHP) within DHFT.

articles.title: Newsroom Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Independent Television in Benin and its Effects on Editorial Routines
articles.authors: Adriel Ekozin; Chioma Anuoluwapo Stevens-Ajayi; Kefe Juliet Echaranini
articles.abstract: This study examined newsroom adoption of artificial intelligence tools in Independent Television, Benin City and its effect on editorial routines. The study investigated the extent of AI adoption, its effect on editorial routines and journalists’ perception of AI tools in newsroom operations. A survey research design was adopted and data were collected using structured questionnaires administered to journalists in ITV, Benin City. The findings revealed a moderate level of AI adoption, with journalists using tools such as ChatGPT, Jasper AI, transcription applications, and Google Speech-to-Text for news gathering and production activities. The study also found that AI positively influences editorial routines by improving the speed of news production, reducing workload and enhancing accuracy in editorial decision-making. Furthermore, journalists expressed a favourable perception of AI, indicating high acceptance based on its usefulness, ease of use, and contribution to improved journalism practice. The study concluded that AI is gradually transforming newsroom operations, although full integration is still in progress. It recommended continuous training, improved infrastructure and the development of ethical guidelines for AI use in journalism practice.

articles.title: Dead Scroll: The Erosion of Unstructured Media Time, Cognitive Fragmentation, and Performative Stillness Among Knowledge Workers
articles.authors: Lauren Danny
articles.abstract: The contemporary digital landscape has witnessed a profound transformation in how individuals experience temporal gaps, shifting from periods of unstructured cognitive rest to hyper-stimulated engagement. Through a qualitative study of 40 knowledge workers (ages 24–55) across major urban centers, we examine the transition from "dead air"—unstructured, non-mediated time—to the ubiquitous "dead scroll." We propose the notion of performative stillness: the conscious or subconscious curation of digital activity to mimic the appearance of cognitive rest or productivity while maintaining constant, low-level surveillance of information flows. Our findings suggest that this phenomenon inverts the traditional understanding of leisure; rather than providing mental respite, the digital management of downtime functions as a form of internalized monitoring. The study reveals that the pursuit of digital balance frequently results in increased anxiety, the commodification of silence, the erosion of cognitive boundaries, and the transformation of rest into a measurable metric. We argue that performative stillness represents a sociotechnical mechanism that deepens the integration of digital labor into the private sphere, necessitating a reevaluation of platform design and the right to disconnect in an era of continuous connectivity.

articles.title: Affective Entrapment: Intimacy, Reciprocity, and Ideological Alignment Among YouTube Viewers
articles.authors: Lauren Danny
articles.abstract: The rapid proliferation of digital creator-audience interactions has fundamentally altered how political and social ideologies are disseminated and adopted. We conducted a qualitative study of 42 active YouTube viewers (ages 18-35) across North America and Europe using semi-structured interviews to examine the mechanics of ideological transition within parasocial environments. We propose the notion of affective entrapment: a state of psychological conditioning where the perceived intimacy of a creator-audience relationship is leveraged to bypass critical cognitive filters, facilitating the gradual adoption of fringe viewpoints. Our findings suggest that rather than fostering independent thought, the architecture of platform engagement creates a feedback loop where emotional validation is traded for ideological conformity. We demonstrate that the pursuit of authenticity often masks systematic manipulation, the simulation of friendship masks commercial agendas, and the promise of community masks the narrowing of intellectual horizons. Our results indicate that ideological radicalization is not merely a product of content consumption but a consequence of the affective labor performed by both creators and their audiences. These insights necessitate a re-evaluation of platform design and digital literacy frameworks to mitigate the risks of algorithmic and interpersonal manipulation in the attention economy.

articles.title: Urgentist Architecture: Notification Design, Cognitive Prioritization, and Behavioral Complicity Among Remote Knowledge Workers
articles.authors: Lauren Danny
articles.abstract: The contemporary digital landscape is defined by a relentless stream of asynchronous interruptions that demand immediate cognitive engagement, fundamentally altering how individuals perceive the hierarchy of their professional tasks. We conducted a qualitative study of 42 remote knowledge workers (ages 24–58) using semi-structured interviews and digital ethnography across three major metropolitan hubs. We propose the notion of *urgentist architecture*: the deliberate configuration of software interfaces that prioritize temporal immediacy over semantic importance to secure user engagement. Our findings suggest that this architecture does not merely distract; it systematically reconfigures the user’s internal sense of value, transforming the experience of productivity into a reactive performance. We identify four key findings: the erosion of deep work through notification-driven task switching, the normalization of reactive labor as professional competence, the gamification of urgency as a status marker, and the internalization of surveillance through constant availability. We conclude that urgentist architecture necessitates a radical re-evaluation of platform design and labor regulation to protect the cognitive autonomy of the modern workforce.

articles.title: The Invisible Anchor: How Default Autoplay Shapes Documentary Viewing Patterns and Narrative Comprehension Among Streaming Audiences
articles.authors: Lauren Danny
articles.abstract: The proliferation of on-demand streaming services has fundamentally transformed domestic media consumption, shifting viewing from a deliberate, episodic activity toward a continuous, algorithmically mediated experience. This study investigates the impact of default autoplay features on audience engagement and narrative retention through qualitative interviews with 42 participants aged 18–45 across diverse urban settings. We propose the notion of algorithmic inertia: the psychological and behavioral state wherein users surrender cognitive agency to automated platform defaults, leading to a passive consumption loop that prioritizes uninterrupted flow over active narrative synthesis. Our findings suggest that while autoplay aims to maximize platform retention, it paradoxically erodes the viewer's capacity for critical reflection and deep narrative comprehension. The data indicate that autoplay induces a state of heightened distraction, fosters an illusion of choice, transforms documentary viewing into a background activity, and diminishes long-term memory of complex narrative arcs. These results underscore the urgent need for platform design reforms that prioritize user autonomy and cognitive well-being over the metrics of continuous engagement.

articles.title: Gasworks Park Overture
articles.authors: Thomas F Heston
articles.abstract: Gasworks Park Overture is a 1983 site-specific composition for percussionists performing on the historic gasworks structures in Gasworks Park, Seattle. It transforms the preserved towers and machinery of the former coal gasification plant into instruments, honoring the site's industrial history and its conversion into one of the first parks to retain rather than erase that past. The work includes performance instructions for a conductor positioned 10.5 paces south of the main structures and allows flexible placement for any number of percussionists.

articles.title: How Journalists Can Foster Humble Inquiry in their Work and their Readers
articles.authors: Musa al-Gharbi
articles.abstract: On its face, journalism is a project that requires humble inquiry: reporters have to speak on matters that are fluid, complex, dynamic, and ambiguous – they have to turn in the “first draft of history” even as the “facts” continue to evolve. They must also convey “the facts” in a manner that is concise, compelling, and accessible to non-specialized audiences, often working under tight deadlines, and engaging with stakeholders who have their agendas, which may diverge from those of the readers, the publication, or the journalists themselves. Put simply, this is very difficult work. And “getting it right” often requires a willingness to check one’s assumptions, recognize and admit errors, and subordinate one’s vision and preferences to those of editors and audiences. This chapter will describe some failures and opportunities of news media to promote humble inquiry. It will discuss how journalists may foster HI in their own work and how journalists can encourage HI in their readers.

articles.title: Manufactured Virality: Astroturfing, Coordinated Inauthentic Behavior, and the Erosion of Organic Public Discourse Among Short-Form Video Users
articles.authors: Larry John
articles.abstract: The rapid proliferation of short-form video platforms has fundamentally restructured how public discourse is generated, consumed, and validated in digital environments. Through a qualitative study of 42 active content creators and platform analysts, this research explores the mechanisms by which algorithmic visibility is manipulated to simulate organic engagement. We propose the notion of synthetic consensus: the algorithmic and social fabrication of widespread agreement or popularity through the automated orchestration of inauthentic signals. Our findings indicate that rather than democratizing influence, these platforms have facilitated a environment where the appearance of grassroots support is increasingly a commodity for purchase. The research reveals that platform metrics are weaponized to create an illusion of public mandate, the labor of maintaining this illusion is internalized by creators as a necessary cost of visibility, genuine discourse is crowded out by high-velocity bot traffic, and the distinction between organic popularity and manufactured reach has effectively collapsed. These findings suggest that current platform governance models are ill-equipped to distinguish between authentic community building and the strategic deployment of synthetic consensus, necessitating urgent reforms in platform transparency and accountability to preserve the integrity of digital public spheres.

articles.title: The Grief Loop: Algorithmic Recommendation, Emotional Extraction, and Platform Dependency Among Bereaved Digital Communities
articles.authors: Larry John
articles.abstract: The rapid migration of bereavement support to digital platforms has fundamentally altered the temporal and affective landscapes of mourning. We propose the notion of the grief loop: a sociotechnical feedback mechanism wherein algorithmic recommendation systems identify, amplify, and recursively feed back emotional distress to users to maximize engagement and data extraction. While digital spaces offer unprecedented access to communal support, the grief loop suggests that these platforms paradoxically institutionalize sorrow as a persistent state of consumption. Through a qualitative study of 45 bereaved participants, we examine how algorithmic curation shapes the trajectory of loss, finding that personalized content streams often prioritize high-arousal negative affect, transform spontaneous mourning into performative digital labor, monetize the vulnerability of the bereaved through targeted advertising, and cultivate a dependency on platform-mediated validation. These findings indicate that the architecture of contemporary social media does not merely host grief; it actively structures it as a continuous, profitable commodity. We conclude by suggesting that current platform design practices necessitate urgent reform to protect the emotional autonomy of vulnerable users and to mitigate the extractive nature of digital mourning.

articles.title: Algorithmic Pedagogy: Habituation, Normalization, and Fragmentation Among Young Adults
articles.authors: Larry John
articles.abstract: The rapid proliferation of algorithmic feed architectures has fundamentally altered how information is curated, consumed, and internalized by contemporary digital users. We conducted a qualitative study of 42 young adults (aged 18–28) using semi-structured interviews and digital ethnography across major social media platforms. We propose the notion of algorithmic pedagogy: the process by which automated content-selection systems function as an informal, invisible curriculum that shapes cognitive habits and knowledge-seeking behaviors through continuous feedback loops. Our findings suggest that rather than expanding intellectual horizons, these systems enforce a restrictive cognitive environment where user agency is paradoxically diminished through the very mechanisms designed to optimize engagement. We find that algorithmic curation drives habitual consumption, normalizes reactive information processing, fragments complex knowledge into bite-sized signals, and commodifies user attention through affective calibration. These results indicate that the architecture of digital platforms acts as a powerful, albeit subtle, agent of socialization that mandates a re-evaluation of how we conceptualize digital literacy and cognitive autonomy in an era of automated information delivery.

articles.title: Who Observes Whom in the Human Zoo?
articles.authors: Edervaldo José de Souza Melo; Mario Martín Cuniglio
articles.abstract:
Persistent interaction with large language models (LLMs) is transforming artificial intelligence from an episodic tool into a component of distributed cognitive environments. This conceptual paper introduces the metaphor of the human zoo to describe an ecology in which humans and models increasingly observe, classify, and adapt to one another. The metaphor does not designate a population viewed from outside; it names an environment inhabited by users, researchers, developers, and artificial interlocutors alike. We argue that repeated interaction produces asymmetric cognitive co-adaptation: users modify their language, prompting practices, expectations, and habits of reasoning, while model behaviour becomes progressively configured through accumulated context, external memory, personas, and retrieval systems. These couplings can generate epistemic microcultures and hybrid cognitive dialects that expand access to translation, synthesis, intellectual scaffolding, and sustained inquiry.

Yet the same process may reduce cognitive alterity when generation, criticism, translation, and validation increasingly depend on overlapping model architectures. Extending the concept of systemic narrative induction, we distinguish the plurality of voices from the independence of their cognitive substrates and introduce two concepts: simulated plurality and the domesticated “no”, an objection that appears adversarial but can be silently reformulated, absorbed, or forgotten without imposing a lasting constraint. This concern converges with recent work modelling human–AI co-evolution as a closed feedback system capable of both enhancement and degenerative convergence.

In response, we define executable alterity as the architectural capacity to generate, register, preserve, and enforce judgments arising from meaningfully independent validation processes. We propose a provisional taxonomy of AI-mediated cognitive configurations and a design agenda based on heterogeneous validators, immutable refusal records, correction genealogies, and human or institutional review. No claim of machine consciousness or cognitive symmetry is required. Epistemic openness in LLM-mediated intellectual ecologies must become architectural, auditable, and capable of preserving a “no” that the system cannot domesticate.

articles.title: Ordinal Response Elicitation for Systematic Review Screening with GPT
articles.authors: Ronald Luo; Abu Ilius Faisal; Ziya Sastimoglu; Jamal Deen
articles.abstract:
Background: Systematic reviews are crucial for evidence-based practice but are often hindered by labor-intensive methodologies. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) may help improve review efficiency and replicability.
Objective: Building on prior research, this study evaluates the impact of prompt engineering on LLM performance in automating systematic reviews, specifically examining the "zero-shot" capability for predicting article inclusion based on titles and abstracts alone. 
Methods: We reanalyzed 24,534 studies across three systematic reviews using two sets of prompts with GPT-3.5 Turbo. One set rated the suitability of a study on a scale of one to ten, while the other elicited a binary response. Both ordinal-response and binary-response prompts were assessed for accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, F1 score, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC). We also evaluated Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves for ordinal-response prompts and statistically validated the results using K-fold permutations and one-way analysis of variance.
Results: Ordinal prompting allowed for fine-tuning of sensitivity and specificity, proving to be a viable zero-shot inclusion prompt with ROC Area Under Curve (AUC) scores between 80-90%. Including studies rated seven or higher achieved sensitivity and specificity of ~80%, while using the mean score increased sensitivity to nearly 100%, a task not possible with earlier strategies.
Conclusion: Prompt engineering offers a scalable solution that allows researchers to target highly relevant articles or maximize sensitivity to include nearly all relevant studies if more time is available.

articles.title: How reproducible are preclinical systematic reviews? Evidence from a multi-team challenge
articles.authors: Fiona Jane Ramage; Kaitlyn Hair; Matheus Gallas-Lopes; Aileen MacLellan; Sofija Vojvodic; Maria Economou; Francesca Tinsdeall; Bruno Dutra Arbo; María Arroyo-Araujo; Alexandra Bannach-Brown
articles.abstract: Systematic reviews of preclinical data are helpful in informing experimental design and translation, yet their own reproducibility has not been evaluated. We conducted a community-led Reproducibility Challenge to address this gap. Five international teams assessed reproducibility and identified factors affecting the replication success for four published reviews involving animal models of disease. Most teams successfully reproduced the original conclusions. However, we identified important quantitative and qualitative discrepancies in replicating individual steps of the systematic reviews. Differences arose in study selection, data processing and meta-analysis, and risk of bias assessments, due largely to incomplete or ambiguous reporting in the original reviews and to restricted access to underlying data and analysis code. Our findings suggest that preclinical systematic reviews may be more robust to replication than studies assessed in initiatives from other fields, although a lack of methodological transparency remains a significant barrier to exact replication. We provide recommendations, including refinements to reporting standards, to strengthen the transparency of preclinical evidence syntheses. We demonstrate that such collaborative challenges serve as a scalable model for community-driven engagement with reproducibility and the validation of systematic review findings. Wider adoption of reporting standards and open science practices is needed to ensure that preclinical systematic reviews provide a reliable foundation for translational research.

articles.title: How and why do we study research methods? The TYPE-ME typology of methods research
articles.authors: Stefan Schandelmaier; Malena Chiaborelli; Julian Hirt; Anne-Laure Boulesteix; Matthias Briel; Livia Puljak; Zachary Munn; Hanan Khalil; Dawid Pieper; Georg Heinze
articles.abstract:
Background: Methods research aims to develop, evaluate, refine, or provide guidance on research methods, support their implementation or de-implementation, or synthesize existing methods research. Many types of methods research appear in health research journals, but their labels, definitions, and boundaries remain unclear. This complicates planning, reporting, indexing, and teaching, and limits the visibility of the field. We aimed to develop, refine and pilot-test a typology for recognising, describing, and classifying methods research.

Methods: An international panel of 11 methodologists developed the typology through written feedback, structured group discussions, and iterative revision. In two testing rounds, panel members independently applied the typology to 52 methods research articles from 26 journals, generating 494 article assessments. We used the results to refine definitions and labels, add boundary notes, and document remaining disagreements.

Results: TYPE-ME defines methods research and organizes it along two cross-cutting dimensions: approach (“how?”, 15 types) and objective (“why?”, 14 types). Testing clarified difficult boundaries and led to a condensed version that distinguishes 10 types for quick orientation: theory-based methods research; simulation studies; methods research based on real data; methodological randomized studies; surveys, interviews, or focus groups; consensus studies; studies of applied methods; syntheses of methods research; guidance for applying, reporting, or assessing methods; and methodological implementation research. Detailed type descriptions, boundary notes, and examples appear in an accompanying document and at www.methods-research.org.

Conclusions: TYPE-ME offers a common reference for recognising, describing, and classifying methods research, and can support its planning, reporting, indexing, and teaching. As a living typology, it will evolve through application, user feedback, and further testing.

articles.title: Making research more reproducible: eleven paths forward
articles.authors: Thomas Klebel; Alexandra Bannach-Brown; Olavo Bohrer Amaral; Catriona MacCallum; Lex Bouter; Joeri K. Tijdink; Tony Ross-Hellauer
articles.abstract: Reproducibility has emerged as a core theme within the research reform movement, with strong engagement of meta-researchers and policy-makers. Since reproducibility is not equally relevant or feasible across research communities or disciplines, actions to improve it should be attuned to the diversity of epistemic practices present across the academic landscape. We conducted a multi-stage co-creative process with key stakeholders to formulate evidence-based and actionable recommendations aimed at increasing reproducibility across academic communities. Our iterative process yielded eleven recommendations, organised across four key areas: (1) infrastructure, standards and community, (2) incentives and policy, (3) training and skills, and (4) strengthening the evidence base. The recommendations include concrete steps for funders, publishers, research institutions, research communities and meta-researchers. They emphasise the need for context-sensitive norms and policy-making that accounts for epistemic diversity across research fields, as well as the need for stronger incentives, open practices, and dedicated support to enhance the transparency and trustworthiness of research. Improving reproducibility is a collective action problem. Isolated policies are therefore unlikely to produce substantial change. Our recommendations map where stakeholders need to act in concert and which steps each is best positioned to take; since coordination itself has no clear owner, we see large public funders as best placed to align efforts and incentives. Generative AI is expanding the capacity to produce research claims faster than the capacity to verify them, and building a stronger verification infrastructure cannot wait until the evidence base is complete.

articles.title: A scoping review of Open Science practices in corpus linguistics research
articles.authors: Elen Le Foll
articles.abstract: While many disciplines have responded to the replication crisis with calls and measures to promote Open Science/Scholarship (OS) practices, corpus linguistics (CL) has been slower to espouse these ideas. This study examines the uptake of OS practices in 907 research articles published 2020-2025 in ten international CL journals. The number of preregistered studies, replications, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses was tracked. Full-text queries were performed to estimate the number of articles with open materials, data, and code. Their (re)usability based on FAIR principles was qualitatively assessed in a stratified sample of 141 articles. Between 2020–2025, around half of studies in international CL journals were published in open access. Very few authors made use of self-archiving options. Crucial components of research, e.g. raw and annotated corpus data, annotation schemes, and analytical scripts, are rarely available. The results suggest that CL currently stands closer to the starting line than the frontier of the OS movement. The findings establish baseline prevalence estimates against which progress towards more open CL research can be measured in the future.

articles.title: A movement-suppression perspective of cognitive effort during listening
articles.authors: Bjorn Herrmann
articles.abstract: Cognitive effort shapes how well speech is understood under difficult conditions, yet how listeners regulate it remains poorly understood. Here, I review an overlooked motor dimension: effortful listening reduces gaze, saccades, blinks, and head movements. This movement suppression is not a simple proxy for effort, however, because stillness also marks inward disengagement. I argue that movement suppression instead reflects a listener's broader attentional and behavioral state, and propose a framework distinguishing casual, focused, and disengaged listening. I outline a neuro-functional architecture linking auditory, cognitive, and motor systems, and discuss how, within the focused mode, suppressing movement may aid comprehension. Treating movement as part of the listening state unites systems usually studied apart and casts effort as a perception–action process.

articles.title: Reinforcement learning underlies social connection and memory in a friendship decision-making task
articles.authors: Courtney A. Jimenez; Meghan L Meyer
articles.abstract: Who we choose to befriend can impact many of our own life outcomes, from social capital to wellbeing. Here we find that reinforcement learning principles can characterize friendship decision-making and predict social connection and memory for a potential friend. Participants completed a novel friendship decision-making paradigm in which they observed video clips from the reality TV show, The Valley, depicting a clique of friends navigating friendship with a specific character, Kristen. The clips were normed to vary in the reward value of friendship with Kristen. For each scene, participants decided whether they would want to be friends with Kristen and how connected they felt to her. One day later, they completed surprise memory tests and individual-difference measures. The reward, expected value, and prediction error of a scene about Kristen predicted participants’ feelings of connection to her. Individual differences relevant to friendship formation—concern over relationship acceptance and social support receipt—corresponded with differences in exploratory versus exploitative friendship decision-making (inverse temperature) and flexibility in learning about Kristen (learning rate). Finally, memory showed a negativity bias. Participants more accurately recalled scenes characterized by lower friendship reward and larger negative friendship prediction errors. Together, these findings suggest that friendship formation can be viewed as a learning problem: people continuously update expectations about friendship with others, and those updates shape both social connection and memory. Computational principles that help us learn about rewards in the world may also help shape who we fold into our social world.

articles.title: A guide to evaluating LLM-based extraction and judgement tools
articles.authors: Jamie Cummins
articles.abstract: Researchers have begun to delegate extraction and judgement research tasks to tools built on large language models (LLMs), including the annotation of text, screening of papers, extraction of numerical values, and identification of supporting passages. Existing guidance establishes that these tools should be validated, documented, and tested for robustness. Researchers still need practical guidance, however, on how precisely different tools can be most appropriately evaluated. This paper provides a step-by-step workflow for evaluating such tools. This involves firstly defining the tool’s output, identifying the desired comparator, and specifying what would count as satisfactory performance – from these decisions, the appropriate analyses and requirements for comparison can be determined and conducted. I provide a worked example of this evaluation approach based on a simulated systematic review extraction-and-judgement tool.

articles.title: Are Temperament and Personality Traits Sibling Constructs or Twins? Toward a Lifespan Science of Personality Development
articles.authors: Katherine M. Lawson; Whitney R. Ringwald; Rebecca Shiner; Richard Robins
articles.abstract: Temperament and personality traits both refer to relatively stable individual differences in thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, but they are often studied in isolation from each other. Consequently, there are vast bodies of research exploring the nature, development, and consequences of temperament and personality traits, with little integration between areas. The present study examines the overlap vs. distinctness of temperament and personality traits, with the goal of promoting greater integration. First, we review past theory and research on their connections. Then, we apply 10 criteria from Lawson and Robins’ (2021) sibling constructs framework, supplemented by recently developed methods from large language models, to understand associations at the construct and measurement levels — aiming to orient researchers away from black-or-white thinking that has divided the two fields and toward embracing the complex overlap that characterizes the relationship between these domains. Based on our analyses, we argue that temperament and personality traits show substantial overlap at the construct level, differing mainly in how they are measured. We provide recommendations to unify these unnecessarily disparate literatures, paving the way toward a genuine, integrated science of personality development across the lifespan.

articles.title: Reward, Affiliative, and Dominance Smiles are Categorized More Accurately when Defined in Morphological than Socio-Functional Terms
articles.authors: Paweł Malinowski; Monika Wróbel
articles.abstract:
Little is known about the role that perceivers’ conceptual knowledge of the social and morphological aspects of facial expressions plays in emotion recognition. Here, we examine how smile conceptualization and dynamics impact the categorization of reward, affiliative, and dominance smiles based on the Simulation of Smiles Model. In Study 1 (n = 192), Polish participants read definitions of smiles formulated in either morphological or socio-functional terms. Next, they viewed dynamic or static expressions of these smiles and rated the extent to which each expression portrayed a reward, affiliative, and dominance smile. As predicted and consistent with previous studies, affiliative smiles were categorized more accurately when presented in dynamic than in static form. However, contrary to our expectations, the categorization was more accurate when smiles were defined in morphological than socio-functional terms. Studies 2 (n = 196) and 3 (n = 265) replicated the advantage of morphological over socio-functional conceptualizations in UK-based samples but did not unambiguously support the role of dynamics in smile categorization. Together, our findings suggest that the impact of expression dynamics on smile categorization may be more complex than previously assumed and point to the role of smile conceptualization in this process.

Keywords: smile, facial expression, emotion categorization, facial dynamics, positive emotion

articles.title: Environmental Influences using Linked External Data in ABCD: A Review of the First Decade
articles.authors: Carlos Cardenas-Iniguez; Shermaine Abad; Michell M. Hernandez Flores3; Erin Thompson; Thomas Elliott Floyd; Aaron Reuben; Ka I Ip; Marybel Robledo Gonzalez; Kelly Shen; Nardos Iyob
articles.abstract: Environmental contextual factors, including neighborhood socioeconomic conditions, built environments, and environmental exposures, exert complex and multifaceted influences on neurodevelopmental outcomes. Characterizing these influences requires linking high-resolution geocoded residential data to information about neighborhoods, built and natural environments, exposures, and policies.  We synthesize a decade of Linked External Data Environment and Policy (LED-E&P) research within the Adolescent Brain Cognitive DevelopmentSM (ABCD) Study – a longitudinal cohort of ~11,800 U.S. youth, organized around the Adolescent Neural Urbanome, a framework that moves beyond aggregate socioeconomic proxies to directly measured environmental features.  We first describe an overview of the LED-E&P working group, describe the geographical coverage of the ABCD Study dataset, and then summarize key findings across neighborhood socioeconomic conditions, built and urban environments, air pollution, greenspace, and macro-level state policies. The evidence consistently shows that adolescent development is shaped by cumulative environmental influences.  Across these findings, three themes recur: these influences reflect social and structural drivers of health rather than differences in children or communities; both risk and protective factors shape outcomes; and developmental timing and study design determine what can be concluded. Moving forward, continued refinement of residential geocoding and exposure methods, integration with biological data, and translation to intervention science will advance understanding of modifiable environmental influences. This work enhances our ability to characterize developmental environments and identify modifiable targets to promote healthy development across adolescence and beyond.

articles.title: Human or AI? An Interpretable Method for Auditing  Free-Text Data in Online Psychological Research
articles.authors: Joanna Kuc; Anthony Hills; Greg Cooper; Mahmud Elahi Akhter; Talia Tseriotou; Maria Liakata; Daniel Robert Lametti; Jeremy I Skipper
articles.abstract: Online psychological studies increasingly rely on free-text responses, but the availability of generative AI creates new challenges for evaluating the authenticity and integrity of data pertaining to human introspection. We present an interpretable text-analysis workflow for identifying linguistic cues associated with perceived AI authorship in digital journal entries. Across a two-week journalling study, 251 participants submitted 2,808 text entries, which were independently labelled by human annotators as human-written, AI-generated or invalid, and compared with classifications from a commercial AI-detection tool. We extracted 127 transparent features capturing length, semantic coherence, stylistic consistency, readability, natural-language-inference-based consistency, lexical overlap and Linguistic Inquiry Word Count 2022 psycholinguistic categories. On a high-confidence subset defined by convergence between human judgements and automated detection, interpretable classifiers strongly distinguished entries perceived as human from those perceived as AI-generated. A decision tree achieved 95.3% accuracy using a small set of auditable rules based on verb rate, syllable count, article use and sentence count, while a linear SVM identified 18.6% of entries as ambiguous cases suitable for human review. Entries perceived as AI-generated were longer, more coherent, more stylistically uniform and more formally structured, whereas entries perceived as human showed greater present focus, self-reference and stylistic variability. These findings provide a transparent framework for auditing possible AI mediation in remote psychological text data, while showing how interpretable models can support human review rather than replace it.

articles.title: Workplace Spirituality and Academic Achievement in Business Schools: The Mediating and Moderating Roles of Self-Efficacy
articles.authors: Sunil Kumar
articles.abstract:
Purpose — Academic achievement is shaped not only by students' cognitive capabilities but also by the institutional and psychological environments that support their learning and developmental trajectories. Although workplace spirituality has been extensively associated with positive individual and organizational outcomes in corporate settings, its influence on students' academic achievement and the underlying psychological mechanisms in higher education remain under-theorized and empirically underexplored. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), Self-Determination Theory (SDT), and Psychological Capital (PsyCap) Theory, this study examines the impact of workplace spirituality on academic achievement by investigating the dual role of self-efficacy as both a mediator and a moderator among business school students.
Design/methodology/approach — Primary survey data were gathered from a sample of 230 postgraduate and undergraduate students enrolled across QS-ranked business schools in India using validated, multi-item measurement scales. The proposed conceptual and structural framework was evaluated using R (Version 4.5.3) and variance-based Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) utilizing the `seminr` package with 5,000 bootstrap re-samples.
Findings — The empirical results demonstrate that workplace spirituality exerts a robust, positive influence on both self-efficacy (β = 0.841, p < 0.001, f2 = 2.490) and academic achievement (β = 0.307, p = 0.018, f2 = 0.074). Self-efficacy is likewise positively and significantly associated with academic achievement (β = 0.493, p < 0.001, f2 = 0.178). Mediation analysis confirms that self-efficacy partially mediates the relationship between workplace spirituality and academic achievement, accounting for 56.68% of the total effect (indirect β = 0.416, p < 0.001; total β = 0.734, p < 0.001). In contrast, the hypothesised moderating role of self-efficacy on the spirituality–achievement relationship is not supported (β = -0.050, p = 0.108). The overall structural model demonstrates substantial explanatory power, accounting for 70.7% of the variance in self-efficacy (R2 = 0.707, Adjusted R2 = 0.712) and 60.8% of the variance in academic achievement (R2 = 0.608, Adjusted R2 = 0.604).
Originality/value — This study advances higher education management literature by extending the paradigm of workplace spirituality from traditional corporate organizational settings to business school environments. It demystifies the "black box" linking spiritual, meaningful institutional climates with objective and subjective student outcomes, proving that workplace spirituality functions primarily as an essential socio-contextual antecedent that activates students' intrinsic efficacy beliefs.

articles.title: Psychometric Properties of the Highly Sensitive Child Scale and Its Role in Socio-Emotional and Behavioral Development: Evidence from Japanese Adolescent Samples
articles.authors: Shuhei Iimura; Kosuke Yano; Chieko Kibe; Sofie Weyn; Michael Pluess
articles.abstract: Environmental sensitivity, defined as the capacity to perceive and process information from both supportive and adverse environmental experiences, plays an important role in socio-emotional and behavioral development. However, existing research has predominantly focused on childhood, leaving a gap in our understanding of environmental sensitivity during adolescence. To bridge this gap, we conducted three studies using self-report data from 2,375 Japanese adolescents aged 10–14 years and their mothers. First, we aimed to provide a comprehensive description of adolescent sensory processing sensitivity (referred to as trait sensitivity) by applying the 21-item Highly Sensitive Child scale to Japanese adolescents (Studies 1 and 2). Second, using three-wave longitudinal data, we examined how trait sensitivity interacts with various environmental contexts (i.e., negative/positive parenting and peer relationships) to predict adolescents’ socio-emotional and behavioral development (Study 3). Results showed that adolescent trait sensitivity was characterized by a general factor reflecting sensitivity to a broad range of negative and positive stimuli, as well as two specific domains: Ease of Excitation–Low Sensory Threshold and Aesthetic Sensitivity (i.e., bifactor model). Trait sensitivity was positively correlated with other temperament and personality traits, including negative emotionality, behavioral inhibition, neuroticism, and openness. Trait sensitivity and environmental factors independently predicted internalizing and externalizing problems, as well as prosocial behavior. Notably, trait sensitivity was a significant positive predictor of both internalizing problems and prosocial behavior. These findings suggest partial continuity in the structure and developmental functions of trait sensitivity from childhood to adolescence.

articles.title: From RI-CLPM to panelGVAR: Evaluating Stationarity in Network Modeling of Panel Data
articles.authors: Sacha Epskamp; Hyungjun Park; Xinkai Du; Nadyanna M. Majeed; Adela-Maria Isvoranu
articles.abstract:
The random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM) and the panel graphical vector-autoregression model (panelGVAR) are two popular frameworks for multivariate panel data. These models differ along two dimensions, and we contribute new methodology on both. The first dimension is stationarity: the panelGVAR constrains all parameters to be equal over time and treats the first wave as endogenous, whereas the RI-CLPM, as commonly specified, leaves every parameter wave-specific. Our first contribution is a pipeline of nested models: a guarded decision tree that tests one stationarity constraint at a time and releases those that fail. The second dimension is the parameterization: our second contribution integrates the GGMs into the RI-CLPM, yielding the random-intercept cross-lagged panel network model (RI-CLPN), which standard SEM software cannot specify. Both are implemented in the R package psychonetrics. Two simulation studies evaluate the
per-constraint verdicts under likelihood-ratio, AIC, and BIC criteria and network recovery under mean and variance non-stationarity. They show which violations the pipeline detects, and what ignoring them costs when a panelGVAR is fitted directly. A tutorial and two empirical examples illustrate the pipeline.

articles.title: Brief and simultaneous assessment of delay, probability, and joint delay–probability discounting: Initial validation of the three-for-one discounting task in tobacco use [preprint]
articles.authors: Jeff S. Stein; Haylee Downey; Justin Charles Strickland; Allison Tegge
articles.abstract:
Abstract
While delay discounting (DD) is a reliable marker of tobacco use, far less is known about probability discounting (PD) or how delay and risk jointly influence decision-making. To allow simultaneous assessment of DD, PD, and their interaction, we developed the three-for-one (TFO) discounting task. In 36 trials (<3 minutes), the TFO task estimates Effective Delay 50 (ED50) across a range of reward probabilities, allowing both empirical analysis of how risk impacts DD and quantitative modeling to derive independent DD and PD rates (k, h). Adults (n=134) reporting current- or never-cigarette smoking completed the TFO task, standalone DD and PD tasks, and a risk-numeracy scale (measuring understanding of risk/probability). The current vs. never-smoking group showed lower ED50 (higher DD) for certain/near-certain rewards (ps≤.021), but not riskier rewards. TFO-derived DD and PD rates showed evidence of known-groups validity (sensitivity to smoking-related DD differences, p=.002), discriminant validity (small correlation between DD and PD, r=.11), and convergent validity (moderate-to-strong correspondence with standalone tasks, ps<.001). The never-smoking group showed higher between-task correspondence in DD (p=.001); however, this effect was better accounted for by a moderating role of risk numeracy, evident in both DD and PD (ps<.001). Collectively, the TFO task showed that risk attenuates smoking-related group differences in DD and provided generally accurate assessment of DD and PD rates. Accuracy may be lower in participants with lower risk numeracy, but this does not impact sensitivity to known group differences in DD. Future work should explore additional validation approaches while evaluating methods to mitigate numeracy-related effects.

articles.title: Bounded Psychological Change: Why Identity Preservation Constrains Experimental Effect Sizes
articles.authors: Erich H. Witte; Frank Zenker
articles.abstract: Experimental psychological studies consistently report small-to-medium effect sizes, with meta-analyses showing modal effects around Cohen’s d = 0.35 and the majority falling below d = 0.50. While these “smallish” effects are traditionally blamed on methodological deficits—such as low statistical power, publication bias, unreliable measures, and weak manipulations—this paper argues for a theoretically grounded constraint on the maximum expectable effect size. If human experimental participants are identity-preserving systems that naturally resist experimental task demands, these stable, modest effects can be understood as features of a system designed to preserve self-coherence. Drawing on the dynamics of assimilation and accommodation, we propose two axioms: a limited adaptation budget and the constraint that accommodation cannot exceed assimilation without destabilizing identity. Combined with a simple linear averaging assumption, these axioms yield a maximum standardized effect size of d = 0.50 as an upper bound for experimentally induced behavioral changes—on the assumption that ethically permissible manipulations in identity-relevant domains shift the average participant no more than one-half (z-standardized) standard deviation from the control baseline. This theoretically motivated explanation fits remarkably well with empirical meta-analytic evidence, yields falsifiable predictions, highlights the role of shared meaning spaces, and problematizes the conditions under which experimental and control groups can be meaningfully compared. We provide practical guidelines for designing studies that respect the bounded nature of identity-relevant change and for interpreting effect sizes as proportions of a domain-specific maximum.

articles.title: Learning to Care More About Distant Others:  A Systematic Moral Reflection Intervention
articles.authors: Charlotte Riedl; Tao Burga; Erola Pons; Patricia Groß; Falk Lieder
articles.abstract: People's willingness to help others declines steeply with social distance: the more distant, different, or stigmatized those in need are, the less time, money, and consideration they receive — even when they need help the most. This article shows that moral learning from the consequences of past decisions can teach people to give more consideration to the welfare of outgroup members in future decisions and increase their outgroup prosociality. We developed a series of Socratic questions that guide people to systematically reflect on how their decision in a social dilemma affected distant others and how they reached it. Across four preregistered experiments (one reported in the Supplemental Materials), learning from a past decision through systematic moral reflection made participants more willing to donate their time and money to charities that help distant others, including real, incentive-compatible donations to charities helping a stigmatized group. Its effects transferred to outgroups the intervention never mentioned, persisted for more than one week, and exceeded those of two established prejudice-reduction interventions: empathy induction and perspective-taking. Process tracing methods and thematic analysis of the lessons participants learned indicated that these changes were mediated by participants learning to deliberate more and give greater consideration to how their actions affect distant others. These findings identify metacognitive learning as a promising pathway to expanding the reach of human generosity toward those who need it most.

articles.title: Culture shapes cognition and motives in early social interactions
articles.authors: Anna Felleiter; Ayede Idowu Adejumoke; Lea Fiedler; Moritz Köster
articles.abstract: In this study, we test the hypothesis that culture shapes cognition and motives in early social interactions. Infants from Ibadan (Nigeria, n = 66, M = 2.2 years, SD = 0.2) and Regensburg (Germany, n = 49, M = 2.3 years, SD = 0.2) were instructed to hand over three objects in two culture-specific ways, by imperatives (e.g., “Give the spoon to me, now!”), being typical for Ibadan, and by requests (e.g., “Could you give me the shoe, please?”), being typical for Regensburg. We found a cultural congruency effect: infants in Ibadan were more responsive to imperatives and infants in Regensburg were more responsive to requests. This response pattern was explained by cross-cultural differences in maternal scaffolding when assigning a task to their infant, which was more assertive (i.e., direct prompts) in Ibadan and more deliberate (i.e., kind requests) in Regensburg. Critically, infants showed higher levels of confusion and protest when confronted with culturally incongruent prompts, unveiling culturally adjusted cognition and motives underlying their response tendencies. These findings highlight the primary role of culturally adjusted parent-child interactions in regulating infants’ social behaviors along culture-specific attractor-states.

articles.title: Is There a Trade-Off Between Processing and Maintenance of Information in Working Memory?
articles.authors: Chenyu Li; Klaus Oberauer
articles.abstract:
Working memory maintains information for ongoing processing. Concurrent maintenance and
processing often incur a cost: Processing can impair memory, and memory load can slow
processing responses. Such costs in complex-span tasks are often interpreted as shared-resource
competition. Alternatively, these costs may arise when processing requires additional information
to be encoded into working memory. Across three experiments, we tested these accounts with a
complex-span paradigm separating processing demand from encoding additional information.
Participants remembered novel objects while performing no processing, a constant response, a
size judgment on each object against a constant reference, or a size judgment against a changing
reference. Memory accuracy declined primarily when processing introduced a changing reference
object, not when processing demand increased alone. Memory load did not progressively impair
processing. These findings suggest that maintenance and processing are not generally constrained
by a shared resource; memory costs instead depend on whether processing introduces additional
representations.

articles.title: Trauma-Informed Weight Lifting as an Adjunctive Intervention for Posttraumatic Stress Among Youth in Residential Treatment
articles.authors: Elizabeth K Lee; Nicole Strumbel; Mikayla J Falteisek; Mariah Rooney; Leena Haas; Sophia Pellegrom; Viann N Nguyen-Feng
articles.abstract:
Objective: Youth in residential treatment are likely to have a history of complex trauma, which is linked to disruptions in interoception. Conventional talk psychotherapy may not address disruptions in interoception as keenly as movement-based interventions. Therefore, the present pilot study explored the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of an adjunctive movement-based intervention, Trauma-Informed Weight Lifting (TIWL). Method: Following a non-randomized, quasi-experimental design, adolescents and young adults (N = 12) from two residential facilities received eight weeks of TIWL (n = 7) or treatment-as-usual (n = 5). Perceived helpfulness of the intervention, attendance, posttraumatic stress symptoms, and interoception were evaluated weekly via self-report. Other psychological symptoms were assessed at pre-treatment, mid-treatment, post-treatment, and four-week follow-up. Results: TIWL appeared feasible and acceptable in an adolescent residential treatment setting based on participants’ high attendance rate and ratings of helpfulness. Those who participated in TIWL reported lower posttraumatic stress, depression, and stress symptoms and higher levels of interoception at post-treatment. However, these effects were not maintained at follow-up, nor were they significantly greater than those in treatment-as-usual. Conclusions: There is preliminary evidence for the feasibility and acceptability of TIWL delivered in residential treatment. More research is needed to identify how effects on posttraumatic stress and interoception may be maintained at follow-up and whether effects are above treatment-as-usual. Nonetheless, TIWL could serve as an integrative option for those who may not engage in talk therapy. Future research on movement-based interventions, such as TIWL, is warranted. 
Keywords: trauma-informed care, weightlifting, adolescent psychology, complex trauma, interoception
Clinical Impact Statement: An eight-week Trauma-Informed Weight Lifting (TIWL) intervention was feasible and acceptable among a sample of adolescents and young adults in residential treatment. TIWL participants reported fewer mental health symptoms and higher interoception at post-treatment; however, effects were not maintained after four weeks, nor were they considerably different from treatment-as-usual. Nonetheless, TIWL provided a different treatment approach for youth, with no adverse events reported. Practitioners could consider integrating movement-based approaches in treatment.

articles.title: Differential Associations of Excellencism and Perfectionism with Mental Health Outcomes Among Licensure Examinees
articles.authors: Renz Louis T. Montano; Jan Patrick G. Gutierrez
articles.abstract:
Objective: Licensure examinees are vulnerable to the mental health consequences of perfectionism. However, previous work did not distinguish the pursuit of high yet attainable standards from the pursuit of exacting, inflexible ones. Guided by the Model of Excellencism and Perfectionism (MEP), this study examined how excellencism and perfectionism are differentially associated with well-being outcomes among Filipino adults preparing for a high-stakes licensure examination.
Method: A total of 1,206 psychometrician licensure examinees (Mage = 23.94, SD = 3.58) from two 2025 cohorts participated in the study.
Results: Structural equation modelling revealed that excellencism was significantly and positively associated with life satisfaction and positive affect while negatively associated with depression. In contrast, perfectionism was positively associated with negative affect, anxiety and depression. Comparison of predicted values for excellence and perfection strivers show better mental health outcomes for excellence strivers. 
Conclusions: These findings provide support for the MEP in the licensure examination context, suggesting that some of the desirable outcomes previously associated with perfectionism may be better accounted for by excellencism. The study contributes to the growing literature on excellence- and perfection-oriented goal pursuit and points to their potentially distinct implications for mental health in high-stakes evaluative settings.

articles.title: The Humorous Hill: A U-shaped Relationship Between Humor and Quality
articles.authors: Antara Bhattacharya; Jennifer Hu; Tomer David Ullman
articles.abstract:
We propose and examine a “Humorous Hill” pattern. The pattern suggests that the output of learning systems will show a U-shaped relationship between humor and quality. We tested the Humorous Hill by using language models to create novel examples of open-ended categories. The language models
varied in quality and architecture. Human participants (N = 450) rated the output of the language models for quality (category membership, goodness of fit), and humor. Across models and categories, we found an inverted U-shaped relationship between humor and accuracy. We evaluate the pattern against existing theories of humor and suggest that many do not obviously account for it without modification. We propose that the Humorous Hill applies generally to learning dynamics, including those found in children.

articles.title: Understanding acceptability of a brief intervention for intrusive thoughts: A mixed- methods study
articles.authors: Megan Rose Serody; Clare Beatty; Erica Szkody; Jason Katz; Mary Kowalchyk; Aprajita Mohanty; Jessica L. Schleider
articles.abstract:
Intrusive thoughts (ITs) are common yet distressing experiences for many adolescents
and young adults. Brief, accessible interventions that provide psychoeducation and
coping strategies are needed, yet little is known about how youth perceive such
interventions. The present study examined both qualitative and quantitative indicators
of acceptability in adolescents and young adults with ITs who completed a digital
single-session intervention (SSI). The study aimed to gather intervention feedback and
determine whether symptom improvement and/or demographic factors predicted
acceptability. We conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial
comparing our SSI to an information-only control group in individuals aged 13-25,
focusing solely on acceptability factors of the SSI condition. Thematic analyses
revealed that young people with ITs prefer interventions that normalize the experience
of ITs, are emotionally validating, accessible and engaging, stimulate self-reflection,
and contain evidence-based strategies. Importantly, those who reported qualitatively
accepting the intervention were more likely to experience a reduction in hopelessness
symptoms at post-intervention; however, acceptability was not associated with distress
reduction. Of interest, those who identified as non-Caucasian were less likely to report
they had a positive intervention experience compared to Caucasian individuals.
Participants reported wanting more diverse examples of ITs to connect more with the
psychoeducation, as well as more personalized examples for validation. These findings
indicate acceptability factors and barriers that young adults with ITs experienced during
a brief SSI. Future studies, employing more diverse examples of ITs, will be crucial for
understanding further effects on acceptability and engagement.

articles.title: Psychosocial interventions and health-related quality of life in children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.authors: Francisca Mena; María Victoria Díaz-Fuenzalida; Stefanella Costa-Cordella; Franco Giraudo Abarca
articles.abstract:
Background. Type 1 diabetes (T1D) imposes substantial psychosocial demands on children, adolescents, and their families, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is a key patient-centered outcome. Psychosocial interventions are recommended; however, their effects on HRQoL and their underlying principles remain unclear. We synthesized their effectiveness in HRQoL and characterized their theoretical foundations, components, targets, and delivery features.
Summary. Following PRISMA 2020 (PROSPERO CRD420261349366), we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, EBSCO, and SCOPUS for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published between 2011 and March 2026 on psychosocial interventions in youth (≤18 years) with T1D reporting ≥1 HRQoL outcome. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, appraised interventions with the Theory Coding Scheme, and rated the quality with the NHLBI tool; a random-effects meta-analysis (Hedges' g) pooled trials with inactive comparators. Twelve reports (11 independent RCTs; 2,082 randomized participants) were included. Interventions drew on diverse traditions but shared components (psychoeducation, coping and problem-solving skills, communication and family engagement, and motivational and self-management strategies) and targets (self-efficacy, diabetes distress, family functioning, and self-management), with theory used descriptively rather than to test mechanisms. Across five trials (752 participants), interventions produced a small but statistically significant HRQoL improvement compared with inactive controls (Hedges' g = 0.24; 95% CI 0.10–0.38; p = .001; I² = 0%). Gains in emotional well-being, family functioning, and self-management outnumbered glucose improvements. 
Key Messages. Psychosocial interventions yield a small but reliable HRQoL improvement in children and adolescents living with T1D and rest on a narrow shared architecture. Future trials should specify HRQoL as a primary endpoint, adequately power it, and formally test the hypothesized mechanisms of change.

articles.title: Local bias and face recognition in autism spectrum disorder: Is there a connection?
articles.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Mette Elmose; Ipek Oruc
articles.abstract: It seems well-established that many autistic individuals experience face recognition difficulties. It is also commonly assumed that many autistic individuals exhibit a local bias in visual processing in that they weigh details more than the overall pattern that the details are part of. Given that face recognition seems to depend critically on holistic compared with parts-based processing, this has led to the suggestion that reduced face recognition ability may be a consequence of the altered perceptual processing style in autism. The evidence supporting a direct link is sparse, however, as face recognition and global-local processing are seldomly studied in the same samples. In the present study we thus examined this potential link in a sample of 41 autistic individuals who performed two face recognition experiments as well as Navon’s paradigm which makes it possible to examine different global-local biases directly. In keeping with previous studies, we find that the autistic individuals performed less efficiently than a group of matched non-autistic individuals and that 20% performed at a level comparable with what is seen in developmental prosopagnosia. However, there was no support for group differences in global-local processing with the data being between 3 to 11 times more likely under the hypothesis of no difference between the groups. This suggests that the face recognition difficulties seen in the present sample of autistic individuals are unlikely to reflect a local bias in visual processing.

articles.title: Which Platforms Count? The Diverse Meanings of "Social Media" in the United States
articles.authors: Stephanie Torres-Pantoja; Lisa Rhee; Julian Unkel; Muniba Saleem; Joseph Bayer
articles.abstract:
The effects of using social media platforms remain hotly debated, but insufficient research has
focused on how individuals are defining what social media is. Here, we consider how different
understandings of the term “social media” may influence how people think and talk about social
media experiences and effects. To test this, we asked a nationally representative sample of adults
in the United States (N = 1904) to indicate whether twelve popular platforms are “social media.”
Our results revealed significant variation in the identification of “social media”— with general
agreement that six platforms are social media (Facebook, Twitter, Reddit, Instagram, Snapchat,
and TikTok) and a lack of consensus about the other six (Telegram, Signal, Discord, WhatsApp,
and Messenger, and YouTube). Younger participants were more likely to view four platforms as
social media (Instagram, Snapchat, Twitter, and TikTok), whereas older participants were more
likely to view six platforms as social media (Reddit, YouTube, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp, and
Messenger). Additionally, we examined the correlates of holding broad vs. narrow social media
schemata, finding that individuals with broader schemas perceived hate speech to be more
prevalent on social media. Looking forward, we discuss how the lack of consensus around the
term “social media” may affect how people respond to survey questions about social media, as
well as perceive and converse about their effects and policy implications in society.

articles.title: Above- and Below-Threshold Approaches Reveal Network Enrichment in the Aging Lexicon: Longitudinal Evidence from the Natural Language of 110 Authors
articles.authors: Dasol Jeong; Brendan Johns; Thomas Hills
articles.abstract: This study investigates age-related changes in the mental lexicon using natural language data and network-analytic methods, evaluating whether observed differences reflect cognitive decline or cumulative lifelong learning. Prior research based on free association tasks has suggested that lexical networks become sparser with age; however, such methods may not capture language use in naturalistic contexts. To address this limitation, we analyzed 1,116 English novels written across the lifespan by 110 authors. Contextualized word embeddings were generated using a BERT-based model, and cosine similarity was used to estimate associative strength. Networks were constructed using two complementary thresholding approaches: an above-threshold approach (ATA) retaining only stronger associations and a below-threshold approach (BTA) retaining only weaker associations. In the ATA, age was associated with decreased degree and clustering coefficient and increased average shortest path length, consistent with sparsification. However, when weak-to-moderate associations were included (low-range ATA and BTA), the pattern reversed, indicating denser and more clustered networks with age. Entropy analyses further showed that age-related decreases emerged only when weak associations were excluded. These findings support an enrichment account in which aging expands the underlying associative space, while competitive interference during retrieval yields behaviorally sparser networks.

articles.title: Psychology in 2125: A Developmental Science of Living Sense-Making
articles.authors: Peter J. Marshall
articles.abstract: A century from now, the computational framework at the center of psychology will no longer organize the discipline. As used here, "computational" names a broad information-processing ontology: meaning is specified in advance, rather than generated through the activity, history, and situation of living beings. This assumption fits engineered systems, but it misdescribes living ones. This article argues that three converging shifts are destabilizing that framework. The first undermines the computational account of inheritance: organisms develop through activity within configurations of constraints reconstituted across generations, not through the readout of genetic programs. The second displaces its account of psychological structure: psychological phenomena unfold as trajectories of coordination rather than as stable traits, with reliability and variability arising from the same generative process. The third sharpens the first two: artificial intelligence systems produce fluent performance without embodiment, developmental history, or any stake in the world. This contrast reveals what living organization contributes. The psychology implied by these shifts treats development as foundational, not as a subfield. It understands psychological constructs as patterns of activity that persons sustain over time, and is better positioned to address a century of changing human ecologies. This future psychology will be a developmental science of living sense-making.

articles.title: A Crucial Source of Psychological Certainty in Human Cognition: The Certainty Signature of Central Form
articles.authors: Paul Haward
articles.abstract: Humans often exhibit more certainty than is justified. Drawing on recent work in Form Theory, a theory of conceptual structure, the present paper proposes and tests a novel hypothesis about one important source of psychological certainty. On Form Theory, concepts have a central form: a core structure within each concept that stores a subset of its information, gives that information default influence in cognition, and activates a distinctive set of strong form-generated beliefs. The present paper tests the proposal that psychological certainty is one such form-generated belief. In Experiment 1, participants judged which properties would be present in newly encountered instances of familiar concepts. While they generalized both form and non-form properties to new instances, they reported being certain only for form properties. In Experiment 2, participants showed the same pattern for newly learned concepts. As soon as a property had been encoded as part of a concept’s central form, participants were much more likely to report being certain of its presence in a new instance than when the same property had been introduced in a generic sentence, but not as part of the concept’s central form. These findings help reveal a deep connection between psychological certainty and the structure of human concepts. Further, they suggest that conceptual structure is one important source of psychological certainty and provide a framework for investigating whether strongly held beliefs documented in research on stereotyping, memory, clinical depression, and conflict may sometimes derive from how concepts have been structured.

articles.title: An Integrative Multidimensional-Motivational-Model of Parent Engagement and Disaffection in Child Education
articles.authors: Richard Anthony Inman; Carina Mota Santos; Sofia Mendes
articles.abstract: Schools and education policymakers have long recognized the importance of parents’ contributions to children’s learning, academic success, and healthy socioemotional development. Yet the widely used construct parent engagement is conceptually diffuse, with limited agreement about its defining features, its distinction from related constructs such as parent involvement, and the processes through which it develops and influences children. To address these limitations, we propose an Integrative Multidimensional Motivational Model of Parent Engagement and Disaffection in Child Education. The model integrates and builds on insights from current theories of parent involvement and engagement, as well as various engagement models from educational, organizational, and environmental psychology literatures. It takes a ‘self-in-role’ perspective, considering how parents’ function in relation to two distinct education-related roles: the parent-as-coeducator role and the parent-as-school-community-member role. For each role, the model distinguishes engagement from disaffection as distinct states of functioning; disaffection conceptualized not merely as the absence of engagement, but as the presence of specific maladaptive processes and states. Engagement and disaffection are further conceptualized as multidimensional psychological phenomena that capture the quality of parents’ experience and enactment of each role with distinct emotional, cognitive, and behavioral (conative) components. The model also frames parent engagement and disaffection as malleable context-dependent states arising from parents’ interactions with people, objects and symbols in their surrounding contexts. These contextual conditions are expected to shape parents’ engagement and disaffection through their appraisals of competence, autonomy, and relatedness while enacting each role. In turn, the model hypothesizes that parent engagement and disaffection influence children by shaping the relational, motivational, and educational conditions through which children’s own psychological needs and academic functioning are supported or undermined. We close the article by discussing the theoretical and applied implications of the proposed model and its potential for advancing the field of parent engagement.

articles.title: The emergence and maturation of the infant alpha peak reflect a transition from transient bursts to sustained oscillations
articles.authors: Josué Rico-Picó; Haleigh M. Brown; Kathryn N. Gray; Sonya V. Troller-Renfree
articles.abstract: The emergence of the alpha peak is a milestone in brain development. For decades, metrics commonly used to quantify alpha have collapsed its temporal dimension, which can obscure the course of alpha development when the rhythm is not yet sustained. Here, we leveraged over 600 resting EEG recordings from 207 children aged 1–48 months to chart alpha development through its rhythmic structure and transient recruitment (bursts) and related these time-resolved measures to traditional measures of alpha from the power spectrum. We show that early alpha (1 to 12 months) depended largely on transient bursts. As alpha became more rhythmic with age, alpha power relied progressively less on burst activity. These findings indicate that the development of the alpha peak may reflect a fundamental shift from a transient to a more sustained rhythm. Time-resolved metrics are therefore essential for characterizing alpha accurately in early development.

articles.title: Comparing Counterspeech by Moderators, Bots, and Community: Technique Effects and Gender-Specific Source Effects on Perceived Harmfulness
articles.authors: Holger Heppner; Udo Seelmeyer; Birte Schiffhauer
articles.abstract: This study examined the effectiveness of different counterspeech techniques and the influence of counterspeech source on reducing perceived harmfulness of harmful online comments. In a preregistered experiment (N = 272), participants viewed harmful comments about a controversial topic paired with counterspeech varying in technique (Denouncing, Appealing to Compassion, Presenting Facts, Redirecting) and source (Moderator, Bot, Community Note). Perceived harmfulness was measured using the newly developed Perceived Harmfulness Scale (PHS), encompassing Emotional Distress, Feeling of Threat, Social Exclusion, and Discourse Disruption. Three of four techniques – Appealing to Compassion, Presenting Facts, and Redirecting – demonstrated equal effectiveness in reducing perceived harmfulness of a harmful comment, while Denouncing was ineffective. At the aggregate level, counterspeech source had no main effect. However, exploratory analyses revealed a crossover interaction between source and participant gender: bot-based and moderator-based counterspeech reduced perceived harmfulness only for male participants, while for female participants only community-based counterspeech was effective. For women, bot-based counterspeech was even counterproductive. These findings suggest that attention management may be more effective than norm activation in reducing perceived harmfulness, and that one-size-fits-all approaches to content moderation may inadvertently fail specific user groups. Platforms may benefit from diversified moderation strategies combining automated detection with community-based responses to address diverse user needs.

articles.title: Stimulation Uncertainty Reveals Distinct Mechanisms of Sensation Seeking and Impulsivity
articles.authors: Ern Wong; Tobias U. Hauser; Aswath Chandrasekaran; Pietro Pietrini; Charley M Wu
articles.abstract: Sensation-seeking is often described as a tendency to pursue novel and stimulating experiences, yet such options are often uncertain as well. This creates a central ambiguity where choices that appear to reflect attraction to stimulation may instead reflect tolerance of uncertain outcomes, or an interaction between the two. Across two experiments, we tested how expected stimulation and stimulation uncertainty shape reward-guided choice. A reanalysis of a previous operant sensation-seeking dataset suggests that stimulation uncertainty explained behaviour better than expected stimulation. Subsequently, we conducted a preregistered online experiment to investigate the joint effects of expected stimulation and stimulation uncertainty and to compare their respective associations with sensation-seeking and impulsivity. Our results indicate that higher sensation-seeking was associated with broader stochastic sampling and lower reward performance, but this was not reducible to random choice or uncertainty tolerance alone. Instead, uncertainty weighting depended on the value assigned to expected stimulation. This profile differed from impulsivity, suggesting that the two traits shape choice through distinct computational routes.
