To monitor the quality and pace of the breathing pattern, a simple controller-based biofeedback mechanism was developed by manually placing the controller on the abdominal area. Twelve adolescent basketball players, three basketball trainers and four psychology experts participated in a formative usability session to assess the current iteration of the game and its readiness for a larger pilot study. A mixed methods analysis was conducted using quantitative Likert scale scores and qualitative thematic analysis. The survey findings showed good overall acceptance across all groups for content and technical appropriateness (M=4.04; SD=0.75). However, qualitative analysis of the emerging themes showed mixed findings, with 54% positive valence and six areas identified for further improvement: 1) instruction clarity, 2) session length optimization, 3) technical stability, 4) visual design, 5) theoretical validation, and 6) practical implementation. These formative findings identify key technical, instructional, and implementation-related refinements required before evaluation in a larger trial.

articles.title: A Review of Replication Attempts Over 88 Years of the American Speech-Language Hearing Association Journal Publications
articles.authors: Andrea Lynn Boh Ford; Jessica Salley Riccardi; Austin Thompson; Helen L Long; James C Borders; Scott R. Schroeder; Alisa Baron; Mariam El Amin; Danika L. Pfeiffer
articles.abstract:
Purpose: This review aimed to determine the prevalence of author-identified replication studies in the field of Communication Sciences and Disorders and examine longitudinal changes in this prevalence across American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA) journals from 1936 to 2024. This review is a conceptual replication of Cook and colleagues’ review of replications in special education journals.
Method: Our data source comprised all 17,986 journal articles published in seven ASHA peer-reviewed journals between 1936 and 2024. We identified 3,903 articles, excluding duplicates, that contained one instance of the word replication or its stem (e.g., replicate, replicable). Two research team members independently screened articles to assess whether the study was a procedural replication aligned with our definition.  One research team member coded each article’s study metadata, CSD topic area, participants, and methods, and replication information, such as type of replication and author-reported replication success. We conducted reliability checks on 20% of articles, with an average agreement of 89.7%.
Results: Of 14,376 published studies for which a replication could have been conducted (i.e., exclusive of non-peer reviewed article types), we found 156 (1.09%) author-identified replication attempts. Most replications were conceptual (n = 122) and, according to the authors’ report, successfully replicated the previous study’s results (n = 77). The replication attempts involved a range of research designs, with experimental/quasi-experimental being the most prevalent (n = 78). Replication attempts were published more frequently over time.
Conclusions: As the first field-wide study to investigate author-identified, methodological replication attempts in CSD, our findings suggest a low rate of attempts, consistent with findings in other fields. Importantly, these replication rates represent the most conservative estimates of replication within the field, as many studies report findings that may build on previous evidence, but do not clearly identify as a direct or conceptual replication and were excluded in the current review. To continue building a cumulative and rigorous evidence base in the field of CSD, researchers should consider sharing their data and materials and completing reporting tools and checklists to clearly detail their methods and analysis processes transparently, enabling future replication. A more extensive investigation is needed to identify replication studies published in other CSD-related journals and to explore whether additional studies that use broader definitions of replication should be considered.

articles.title: Investigating the longevity of real-world memory following a smartphone intervention in older adults: A multi-year follow-up study
articles.authors: Bryan Hong; Eliza McCann; Miranda Chang; Morgan Barense
articles.abstract: Our ability to recollect details from personal past events tends to decline with age, which can affect how we act in the world, communicate with others, and understand ourselves. HippoCamera is a neuroscience-guided smartphone application that aims to mitigate these age-related memory changes by guiding users to record and review cues for real-world events using established mnemonic strategies. Previous work demonstrated improved episodic recollection and enhanced hippocampal activity for events reviewed using HippoCamera. Here, we followed up with 25 older adults 3.5 to 6 years after their participation in a HippoCamera study, using a mixed-methods approach to assess the longevity of these memory benefits. Participants reported greater subjective re-experiencing for events that were previously reviewed using HippoCamera relative to events that were only recorded but never reviewed. Further, participants reported greater subjective re-experiencing for events recorded using HippoCamera compared to events that were cued with calendar entries from a comparable time period. Using semi-structured interviews, we also explored the experience of using HippoCamera itself and reminiscing upon their past recorded events. Participants spoke to the benefits of HippoCamera not only for episodic memory, but more broadly to their daily lifestyle and activities, and their sense of meaning and well-being. Participants also reflected upon their attitudes and beliefs both towards HippoCamera and their own memory as it changes with age. Altogether, these results demonstrate the broad and long-lasting effects of a smartphone-based tool that improves memory for real-world events and enriches how older adults relate to their own past experiences.

articles.title: Reading Tiramisu in Czech and English: Robust Processing Speed Differences in Translation Equivalent Stimuli
articles.authors: Jan Chromý; Markéta Ceháková; Michael Ramscar
articles.abstract: Cross-linguistic studies of reading have documented broad similarities across languages, yet the extent to which first-language (L1) reading processes differ once structural confounds are minimized remains unclear. We conducted self-paced reading experiments in English and Czech using tightly aligned translation-equivalent sentences, enabling a direct comparison of L1 reading under parallel input conditions. Matched groups of English and Czech L1 speakers (N = 176 per language) showed near-identical comprehension accuracy but robust differences in processing speed: reaction times (RTs) were reliably faster in English than in Czech, a pattern that persisted after controlling for word length and surprisal. At the same time, the effects of classical predictors such as length and surprisal were directionally similar across languages, consistent with universal reading mechanisms. Our analyses suggest two complementary explanations for the observed cross‑linguistic differences. First, Czech exhibits higher information density than English, which—under conditions that prevent skipping and regressions—manifests as slower per‑word reading. Second, surprisal was distributed differently across the two languages: in Czech, surprisal was markedly higher at sentence onset and decreased more steeply over word position, amplifying early‑sentence processing demands. These findings indicate that while core reading processes are universal, language‑specific typological properties shape how information is packaged and distributed across the sentence, yielding systematic cross‑linguistic differences in processing speed. The results parallel cross-linguistic findings on speech rate and support an emerging framework in which reading adapts to the informational structure of the language being processed.

articles.title: The Dynamic Hierarchy of Personal Space Regulation and its Modulation by Childhood Traumatic Experiences
articles.authors: Lorenzo Lucherini Angeletti; Bianca Ventura; Giovanni Castellini; Andrew Nicholson; Ferdinando Galassi; Angelika Wolman; Josh Goheen; Sarah Masoumi; Andrea Buccellato; Benedetto Farina
articles.abstract: Personal space (PS) regulation represents a core component of socio-affective functioning, requiring the dynamic coordination of perception, affect, and behavior. Yet how these components are hierarchically organized and how adverse childhood experiences modulate this organization remain unclear. To address these gaps, 57 healthy participants underwent a computerized audiovisual stop-distance paradigm. Participants were presented with social (angry, neutral faces) and non-social (ball) stimuli approaching at two speeds. Across trials, participants stopped the stimulus at their preferred distance and rated perceived distance, perceived speed, discomfort, and threat. Bayesian multilevel modeling revealed a hierarchical Perception→Affect→Behavior architecture sustained by two functionally distinct pathways: a spatial–behavioral pathway in which perceived distance directly predicted interpersonal distance, and a temporal–affective pathway in which perceived speed predicted behavior primarily through affective elaboration. Childhood trauma was quantified using the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) as a continuous measure. First, higher CTQ scores were associated with broader interpersonal distances across conditions and with amplified perceptual-affective reactivity to fast approach dynamics. Second, childhood trauma selectively restructured the spatial–behavioral pathway when stimuli were perceived as distant, shifting regulation from bodily discomfort toward anticipatory threat evaluation, while the temporal–affective pathway remained preserved. Third, higher childhood trauma scores were associated with reduced habituation of affective and behavioral responses across repeated trials. These findings characterize PS as a hierarchical dynamic regulatory system in which spatial and temporal cues engage distinct functional routes. Childhood adversity emerges as a systemic modulation that shifts the global regulatory threshold, reorganizes pathway-specific dynamics, and reduces temporal flexibility.

articles.title: Assessment of food cravings and food addiction
articles.authors: Adrian Meule
articles.abstract: This chapter briefly defines the terms food craving and food addiction and describes the most common assessment methods. These include self-report instruments such as the Food Cravings Questionnaires, the Food Craving Inventory, the Craving Experience Questionnaire, and the Yale Food Addiction Scale as well as interview measures such as the Food Addiction Symptom Inventory. It concludes by highlighting the overlaps between food craving measures and measures of food addiction as well as related constructs.

articles.title: The Morality-Effectiveness Disconnect of Pro-environmental Behaviors
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Hege Landsvik
articles.abstract: Not all pro-environmental behaviors are created equal—some are vastly more effective at mitigating climate change than others. Do people judge the more effective behaviors as proportionally more moral? Five main and six supplemental studies (N = 9,247) across five countries reveal a robust morality-effectiveness disconnect: pro-environmental behaviors that rank better on objective climate-mitigation potential rank worse on individual moral judgments. Laypeople fail to predict this pattern, believing that a positive relationship exists. Further, labeling behaviors by climate impact category reduces the morality-effectiveness disconnect, and detailed impact information reverses it and increases policy endorsement of more effective behaviors over less effective behaviors. While the disconnect primarily stems from effectiveness misperceptions that accurate information can mitigate, we find that personal support for less effective behaviors plays an additional role. Thus, people's moral intuition for climate action appears miscalibrated: moral cognition can undermine the collective welfare that such cognition should presumably promote.

articles.title: Beyond Universality: Do All Adolescent Minds Benefit from Mindfulness?
articles.authors: Maria Anna Wasylkowska; Pawel Holas; Dorota Kobylinska
articles.abstract: Despite the rapid global implementation of school-based mindfulness trainings (SBMTs), empirical findings regarding their effectiveness in children and adolescents remain inconsistent. Large-scale trials and recent meta-analyses have challenged early optimism, raising critical questions about for whom, under what conditions, and through which mechanisms SBMTs may be beneficial. This paper provides a synthesis of key factors, grounded in both theory and practice, that may help explain why mindfulness interventions vary in their effectiveness for adolescents. Based on existing research and insights from implementing SBMTs in school settings, we examine four interrelated domains: (1) curriculum characteristics, with particular attention to the role of embodied, mind–body practices and practice dosage; (2) the contribution of teachers, including personal mindfulness practice, embodiment, and relational engagement; (3) developmental considerations related to age, metacognitive capacity, and ethical challenges in assessment; and (4) contextual influences at the level of the school ecosystem and broader sociocultural environment. We argue that assuming universal effectiveness can overlook important sources of variability and may help explain the null or even negative outcomes reported in some studies. By reframing SBMTs as context-sensitive, developmentally attuned, and relationally embedded practices, this paper advances a conceptual framework to guide future research, intervention design, and implementation in educational settings.

articles.title: Enacting Open Science Values in Qualitative Leadership Research: Existing Practices and Future Directions
articles.authors: Camille Endacott; Brent Reed; Crystal Nicole Steltenpohl
articles.abstract: The open science movement has gained considerable momentum in advancing the transparency, credibility, and rigor of scientific research across disciplines. Within this broader landscape, leadership scholars have played a prominent role in developing formal guidance to strengthen open science practices in organizational research. To date, most recommendations have focused on quantitative research rooted in post-positivist traditions. However, qualitative scholars working from interpretivist perspectives share core values such as openness, integrity, and reproducibility with open science and enact them through practices grounded in inductive, context-sensitive inquiry. Bringing these two conversations into closer dialogue offers meaningful opportunities for both domains. Leadership research provides a particularly generative context for this exchange, as qualitative methods have influenced the field by illuminating the socially constructed and value-laden nature of leading. Drawing on these contributions, we present a set of 12 established practices through which interpretivist qualitative researchers have historically embodied open science values in leadership research, followed by six additional practices that can further enhance the openness, integrity, and reproducibility of interpretivist scholarship. By articulating how open science principles can be enacted in qualitative paradigms, we show that leadership scholars are well-positioned to extend the open science conversation across methodologies and communities of practice.

articles.title: (Computation of) the Standardized Mean Difference in Clinical Trials Should be Standardized
articles.authors: Alexander O. Crenshaw
articles.abstract: The standardized mean difference (SMD) is widely used in psychology clinical trials to convert intervention effect estimates from raw units to a common scale, enabling comparison across settings. However, multiple operationalizations of the SMD are possible for clinical trial data, with large potential impacts on estimate magnitudes. In this commentary, I review practices for operationalizing the SMD in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology and other journals that publish results of clinical trials. I find that only one-third of studies report sufficient information to determine the operationalization. Among those, the operationalization varies widely, threatening the SMD’s utility in providing a common scale. Given the common goals and design elements across many trials, it is feasible to establish a default operationalization for the SMD’s standardizer. I outline eight desirable SMD properties and evaluate each option against these properties. The pooled baseline standard deviation meets seven of eight, far more than any alternative, with its main limitation being susceptibility to inflation from restrictive inclusion criteria. I conclude that raw effect estimates should be divided by the pooled baseline standard deviation as a default, one-size-fits-most choice. Adopting this standard will help the SMD meet its promise as a standardized metric, improving comparability of results across different measures, outcomes, studies, and populations. I also provide reporting recommendations to improve transparency and enable re-computation using alternative standardizers when needed.

articles.title: Understanding the morality of unbelievers: Secular beliefs about right and wrong in ten countries
articles.authors: Roosa Haimila; Tiina A M Parkkinen; Eva Kundtová Klocová; Everton de Oliveira Maraldi; Hugh Turpin; Miguel Farias; Valerie van Mulukom
articles.abstract: Many people around the world believe that to be moral, one must believe in God. However, individuals who do not believe in God also hold distinct ethical beliefs. Similar to theists, non-theists in different cultures may share overarching narratives about morality and what it is founded upon—a possibility that remains understudied. In the present research, we utilised open-ended survey data to explore what non-theists from ten countries (N = 996) described as the basis of their views on right and wrong. We also investigated how different beliefs about morality clustered together. The findings show diversity but also point towards cross-culturally recurring patterns in non-theistic beliefs and belief clusters concerning 1) important moral principles and 2) perceived sources of morality. We furthermore discuss country-specific findings, such as the importance of ‘conscience’ for Turkish and Czech participants and ‘cultural Christianity’ in the Danish sample. Altogether, the results support research indicating that a lack of belief in God does not entail moral relativism and question views on non-theists primarily seeing morality as self-constructed. Instead, our findings point towards a more prominent role of social interaction and ‘social contract’ in views about the basis of right and wrong. In light of the results, we suggest that predominant ways of measurement in moral psychology may currently obscure diversity in non-theistic moral outlooks, such as more communal secular ethics. The main limitation of the research is convenience sampling. We therefore encourage future work to utilise representative samples to explore differing secular moralities and their predictors.

articles.title: Interpreting FMS and SSQ Cybersickness Ratings via User Tolerance in Virtual Reality
articles.authors: Jonathan Kelly; Michael Dorneich; Stephen Gilbert
articles.abstract: Cybersickness remains a persistent challenge limiting the usability of virtual reality (VR), yet commonly used subjective measures such as the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) and the Fast Motion Sickness (FMS) scale are often difficult to interpret in terms of user outcomes. In particular, there is limited guidance on how specific values on these scales relate to user tolerance or the likelihood that users will discontinue a VR experience due to discomfort. This work addresses this gap by calibrating cybersickness severity interpretations against early termination of a VR experience. In Study 1 (N = 183), participants played an immersive VR game for up to 20 minutes and were free to terminate the experience at any time. Using a Behavioral Risk Banding (BRB) framework, logistic regression linked a modified 0-10 version of the FMS (FMS-10) and post-exposure SSQ scores to dropout probability, yielding behaviorally grounded risk severity bands (mild, moderate, severe, extreme). Survival analyses then showed how these bands mapped onto tolerance over time, revealing a transitional region marked by heightened individual variability. Study 2 (N = 304) evaluated the robustness of these categories across variation in VR content and mitigation context by applying the Study 1 thresholds without re-estimation. Although absolute dropout risk varied, the ordering and behavioral meaning of severity categories were preserved. Together, these results provide a practical, behaviorally grounded framework for interpreting cybersickness ratings in terms of user tolerance and usability across VR contexts.

articles.title: Creativity Geometry: Recursive Creative Self-Improvement Through System-3 Metacognitive Scaffolding
articles.authors: Juan Carlos Chávez-Autor
articles.abstract: Human creative cognition and frontier artificial intelligence increasingly confront the same higher-order problem: how to generate possibilities, evaluate them, integrate feedback, preserve meaningful diversity, and use previous experience to improve future creative activity. Existing accounts often isolate one part of this process. Creativity research commonly emphasizes novel and useful products; dual-process theories emphasize associative and analytic modes; artificial-intelligence research emphasizes generation, self-correction, agents, tools, or self-modification. None of these alone explains when recurrence becomes recursive creative self-improvement. This Conceptual Analysis introduces Creativity Geometry, a meta-theoretical framework centered on Generation, Reflection, Integration/Iteration, and Metacontrol (GRIM) across Time. These are not proposed as independent modules or a literal mathematical law, but as interdependent functions defining the relational shape of creative transformation. System-3 denotes the metacognitively governed configuration that regulates when to broaden search, constrain it, reorganize representations, seek feedback, continue, or commit. Novelty, usefulness, and diversity (NUD) independently evaluate the resulting creative repertoire; diversity is treated as a set- and population-level condition that protects future option value. In biological cognition, the framework is grounded in creative metacognition, embodied valuation, default-executive network cooperation, confidence and error monitoring, and neuromodulatory regulation of effort, persistence, exploration, and switching. In artificial systems, System-3 is a functional analogue involving generators, critics, memory, integration, telemetry, and bounded control, without implying consciousness or organismic purpose. Evidence from large-language-model self-correction, code refinement, automated scientific discovery, creativity benchmarks, and human-AI collaboration reveals both the promise of recursive workflows and the risks of evaluator dependence, homogenization, and recursive collapse. Creativity Geometry defines recursive self-improvement as improvement in the scaffold governing future creative cycles, demonstrated through independent evaluation, transfer, stability, traceability, and preserved diversity. The result is a conceptual foundation for the science of human creativity and the responsible development of recursively improving AI.

articles.title: The Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ):  Measuring Individual Differences in Song Listening
articles.authors: Dominique T Vuvan; Julia Cannistraro; Rachel Goodkind; Megha Sharda
articles.abstract: Recent years have seen a significant increase in the use of songs, which contain an integrated music/language signal, as experimental stimuli. This has created a need for standardized tools to measure individual differences in song perception. The current article reports the development of the Lyric Focus Questionnaire (LFQ), which measures the degree to which a song listener’s cognitive resources are oriented towards the lyrics versus the other musical features (i.e., pitch, rhythm, timbre). In Study 1, we used exploratory factor analysis to reduce 121 candidate items down to 12 items for the LFQ. In Study 2, we used confirmatory factor analysis and internal consistency measures to ascertain the unidimensional structure of the LFQ. In Studies 3 and 4, we demonstrated that the LFQ is correlated to comprehension of lyrics but not to the ability to exactly recall lyrics. In Study 5, we aggregated data from the first four studies to create initial norms for the Lyric Focus Questionnaire and to explore discriminant validity between Lyric Focus and musical and literary activities with more statistical power than in each study alone. The LFQ is presented as a practical, valid, and reliable tool for researchers interested in the relation between music and language.

articles.title: Self-Construal, Sense of Belonging, Perceived Match, and Persistence Intentions: Exploring Intersecting Identities and Moderation Effects
articles.authors: Ordene Edwards; Maci DeMott
articles.abstract: Prior research has examined the relationships among self-construal, sense of belonging, perceived match, persistence intentions, and demographic factors. However, investigations often overlook the intersecting identities of race, gender, and generation status. Furthermore, little is known about how these demographic factors moderate the relationship between these psychosocial factors and persistence intentions. This study explored self-construal, perceived match, sense of belonging, and persistence intentions at the intersection of race, gender, and generation status. We also examined how these characteristics influence the relationship between these psychosocial factors and persistence intentions. Participants were introductory psychology students (N = 1,496). Three-way ANOVAs revealed one significant three-way interaction for interdependent self-construal, favoring Hispanic continuing-generation (CG) female students over Hispanic CG males, albeit with a small effect size. Additionally, moderation analysis revealed that independent self-construal more strongly influenced persistence intentions among first-generation students than CG students. Theoretical and practical implications of the findings are discussed.

articles.title: Relative weighting of visual and auditory cues in street-crossing decisions with age-related macular degeneration
articles.authors: Daniel Oberfeld; Patricia R. DeLucia; joseph kearney; Melissa Cloutier; Anna M. Jilla; Audrey Taylor; Charles C. Wykoff; Robin Baurès
articles.abstract: We investigated street-crossing decisions in individuals with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) compared to a group with normal vision, using highly realistic visual and acoustic simulations of a vehicle approaching a pedestrian. Participants pressed a button at the last safe moment they could safely start crossing the street. The vehicle was presented visually, auditorily, or both concurrently. We present a novel analysis method for estimating the relative importance of visual and auditory cues for the crossing decision. In single-modality conditions, cue weights indicated that responses were associated not only with the vehicle's arrival time (i.e., gap duration), as it would be if decisions were based on an unbiased estimate of the arrival time, but also with the vehicle’s spatial distance, optical size, acoustic vehicle source intensity, and with time elapsed after the trial start. In the audiovisual condition, auditory and visual cues were associated with the responses. Results are largely compatible with cue weights in arrival time estimates made by the same participants, reported in a previous paper. The cue weights showed minor differences between the groups with AMD and normal vision. Analyses of the mean judged shortest safe gaps and their intraindividual variability showed effects of vehicle speed, source intensity, and size, compatible with the cue weights and TTC estimation results from our previous paper, but again with minor differences between the two groups. However, the proportion of safe crossing decisions was lower in the AMD group, due to a slower walking speed. Our study provides important insights into the decision-making in crossing decisions and shows that AMD had a surprisingly small effect on such decisions.

articles.title: Meditation Fosters Bonding and Cooperation with Humanity and All Forms of Life
articles.authors: Liudmila Gamaiunova; Harvey Whitehouse
articles.abstract: Altruism in social species, including humans, typically favors genetically close individuals. But humans also show altruism toward non-related individuals who share religious beliefs, ethnic origins, or national identities. This study explores whether Buddhist contemplative training fosters identity fusion—a strong, kin-like psychological bond—with humanity at large and all forms of life on Earth. In a cross-sectional design, 418 Buddhist meditation practitioners and 418 age and gender-matched non-practitioners completed measures of identity fusion and related mechanisms, such as perceived shared biology and empathy-related affective states. Participants also performed a semi-hypothetical donation task. Results showed that practitioners reported significantly higher identity fusion with both humans and animals and made larger donations to humanitarian and animal-protection charities. Meditation impacted underlying mechanisms differently: perceived shared biology increased more for animals, while empathy-related states increased more for humans. Both mechanisms mediated the link between contemplative practice and identity fusion. In turn, identity fusion partially mediated the relationship between meditation and charitable giving, suggesting that fusion with the target group influenced altruistic behavior. These findings suggest that contemplative training may help to extend the cooperative benefits of identity fusion with unrelated individuals, and even with other species.

articles.title: Cognitive functions in childhood apraxia of speech: A scoping review
articles.authors: Shina Jinn Cook; Edwin Maas
articles.abstract:
Purpose: Children with childhood apraxia of speech (CAS) often have co-occurring difficulties in language, learning, motor, and sensory function, but the neurological bases of the disorder are debated. A domain-general theory suggests that CAS may involve cognitive domains beyond motor-speech function. The purpose of this scoping review is to evaluate the state of the evidence describing cognitive functions in CAS and identify gaps to guide future research in elucidating the nature of the disorder.  

Method: The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for scoping reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines were used. Five databases were searched to identify articles, supplemented with citation chasing. Included articles were charted by purpose, design, and CAS diagnostic confidence.  

Result: Seventeen articles published between 1979 and 2022 met inclusion criteria following full-text review. Studies primarily examined sequential processing, procedural learning, working memory, and executive function. Most studies used comparative designs. Across studies, participants with CAS demonstrated difficulties on cognitive tasks compared to controls or normative data. Variability in participants, measures, methodology, and diagnostic confidence limits the generalizability of findings.  

Discussion: Despite methodological variability, findings broadly support the investigation of domain-general cognitive mechanisms in CAS. Further research using replication, longitudinal designs, and ecologically valid assessments is needed to delineate the relationship between CAS and cognitive functioning.

articles.title: High-frequency visual stimulation can increase medial temporal lobe ripple oscillation density
articles.authors: Julian Keil; Victor Hernandez-Urbina; Liam Doherty; Hamed Bahmani; Martin Holtkamp; David Steinbart; Alexandra-Dikorey Diall; Jonas Hebel; Christian Brandt; Thomas Cloppenborg
articles.abstract:
Background: Flickering visual stimulation can evoke neural oscillations, which can influence ongoing brain activity. Electrophysiological recordings of neural oscillations in the ripple band (80-180 Hz) showed that these high-frequency oscillations occur in the neocortex and the hippocampus, that they phase-synchronize across long distances, and that ripple oscillations in the neocortex often precede those in the hippocampus during wakefulness. It is therefore possible that the neocortical ripple oscillations propagate beyond sensory areas to the hippocampus, inducing ripple oscillations. 
Methods: To test this hypothesis, we conducted an experiment (N = 8) in humans, using ultra-high frequency visual stimulation (UHV-stimulation) to evoke ripple oscillations recorded through electrodes implanted in or near the hippocampus. Although hippocampal ripple oscillations, so-called sharp-wave-ripples (SWRs), mostly occur during quiet rest or slow-wave-sleep, we aimed to increase their abundance using visual stimulation during wakefulness. We hypothesized that UHV-stimulation would increase the number of SWRs relative to an eyes-open resting-state baseline. 
Results: In line with this hypothesis, we observed significantly more SWRs per second during periods of stimulation compared to a resting-state baseline before and after the stimulation. 
Conclusion: This indicates that UHV-stimulation can be used as a safe noninvasive tool to influence SWRs, which offers the potential to improve memory.

articles.title: “How Do You Feel?” Direct Valence Measurement Enables the Detection of Affect Shift Dynamics as Powerful Predictors of Psychological Well-Being
articles.authors: Carmen Goicoechea; Pandelis Perakakis
articles.abstract: Valence is central to affective experience yet remains poorly operationalized in emotion science. Most research infers valence by categorizing discrete emotions as positive or negative, which may conflate distinct aspects of emotional experience. On the other hand, direct bipolar valence measurement—asking individuals "How do you feel?" on a continuum from negative to positive—allows participants to integrate contextual complexity into their affective reports. Critically, this approach also enables the detection and quantification of transitions between positive and negative affective states, opening new possibilities for studying affect dynamics. We tested whether metrics quantifying these directional transitions predict psychological well-being more effectively than traditional intensity-based measures. Across three ecological momentary assessment datasets with 345 participants and over 30,000 assessments, the positive to negative affect shift ratio—quantifying the propensity to transition from positive to negative affect—showed stronger predictive associations with well-being outcomes than means and standard deviations derived from the same valence scale. This pattern persisted across LASSO regression, hierarchical regression, and relative importance analyses, and remained robust even with only 3 daily assessments. These findings demonstrate that direct valence measurement offers both theoretical advantages by respecting participant-integrated experience and empirical advantages by enabling more predictive dynamics metrics, while remaining practical for clinical applications.

articles.title: Testing the impact of filtering harmful posts: A randomized-controlled trial with 100.000 users on Nextdoor
articles.authors: David Joachim Grüning; Matthew Katsaros
articles.abstract: We investigate the effectiveness of an intervention designed to filter offensive content on the local social media platform Nextdoor. The intervention, commonly used across large social platforms, was tested through a randomized controlled trial involving 100,000 people over nine months. We evaluated whether filtering content impacted fifteen different measures of platform behavior including views of offensive posts, visits to the platform, content consumption, and content production. This randomized-controlled experiment was an advanced followup-study of a Nextdoor-study (Katsaros et al., 2023) conducted a year before, showing mostly null effects of the intervention. In this study, the results showed a significant reduction in two target outcomes - views of offensive posts and comments - in the treatment group compared to the control group. However, as in the past Nextdoor-experiment, we observed no significant effects of the intervention on the thirteen measured outcomes between groups. This study provides empirical evidence on the impact of a prominent and commonly used intervention and highlights its limitation, demonstrating the complexity of effectively moderating online platforms.

articles.title: Interpersonal Extrinsic Dysregulation: Rethinking Emotion Dysregulation Across Childhood
articles.authors: Evelyn Mary-Ann Antony; Sarah A Walker; Nadin Beckmann
articles.abstract:
Interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation refers to persistent yet miscalibrated or dysregulating attempts to influence others’ emotional states, and 2) pervasive avoidance of emotionally charged interpersonal situations. We conceptualise interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation as distinct from intrapersonal emotion dysregulation and related interpersonal phenomena (e.g., co-rumination, empathy, and parentification), as it specifically concerns the child's role as a regulator of others’ emotions and the systematic miscalibration or avoidance of this regulatory function. This paper presents an integrative developmental framework that conceptualises interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation as a reciprocal process embedded within emotional exchanges across family, peer, and educational contexts. Drawing on attachment theory, social-cognitive learning theory, and reinforcement learning perspectives, we propose that maladaptive interpersonal regulatory orientations emerge through the cumulative effects of early relational experiences, observational learning, and contingently reinforced emotional behaviours. We further examine how stressors across multiple domains, including family conflict, academic pressures, and broader socio-cultural inequalities, may interact over time to exacerbate dysregulation and undermine psychosocial functioning. Extending this across childhood, we outline how interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation may manifest differently from early to late childhood as regulatory capacities and interpersonal demands evolve. We conclude by identifying key priorities for future research, including the need for longitudinal, multi-informant, and observational approaches to clarify the developmental origins, differentiation, and consequences of interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation. By providing the first integrative framework for this construct, this paper aims to advance understanding of children's interpersonal emotion regulation and its role in socioemotional development.


Keywords: emotion dysregulation, interpersonal extrinsic dysregulation, emotion development

articles.title: Measuring Reputation and Identity Effects in Multiple Rater Assessments: Guidelines for Specifying Trait Reputation Identity Models
articles.authors: Lukas Aaron Knitter; Michael Eid; Tobias Koch
articles.abstract: Multirater assessments are widely used in psychology to seperate what targets report about themselves from what others perceive about them. The Trait–Reputation–Identity (TRI) model provides a prominent modeling approach for this purpose, but applications of the model often yield improper solutions, including negative variances and weak or inadmissible factor loadings. We argue that these problems arise because the original TRI model does not sufficiently distinguish between different rater types and designs. Building on stochastic measurement theory, we show that TRI model components have different meanings depending on whether observers are interchangeable or structurally different raters. For interchangeable observers, the common observer perspective is already represented by an observer-trait factor. Consequently, the reputation effect cannot be modeled as a higher-order factor. Moreover, identity and reputation effects must be estimated in separate models. For structurally different observers, different TRI models can be specified to answer different substantive questions. We derive different design-oriented TRI models, define variance components for trait, reputation, identity, and rater-specific effects, and illustrate the approach with empirical examples. The proposed framework clarifies the interpretation of TRI effects and provides practical guidelines for specifying TRI models.

articles.title: National Predictors of Conspiracy Beliefs: A Machine Learning Analysis of Cross-Country Data
articles.authors: Sinan Alper; Caspar J. Van Lissa; Karen Douglas; Robbie M. Sutton
articles.abstract: Conspiracy beliefs vary widely across nations, yet their societal predictors remain poorly understood. Applying machine-learning meta-analytic techniques, we simultaneously examined 18 national-level developmental and cultural factors and ranked their relative importance in predicting conspiracy beliefs. Across six large cross-national datasets (total N = 178,789; 72 countries), the best-performing model (MetaForest) explained 43% of variance in test data. Corruption was the strongest predictor, followed by power distance, reading proficiency, individualism, mathematics proficiency, human development, GDP, and science proficiency. Conspiracy beliefs were most prevalent in societies marked by higher corruption and power distance, and lower educational performance, individualism, and socioeconomic development; developmental indicators generally outranked cultural ones, and dimensions such as WEIRDness, uncertainty avoidance, and long-term orientation mattered little. By integrating developmental and cultural predictors in a single framework, this study offers the most comprehensive test to date of national correlates of conspiracy beliefs and demonstrates the value of machine-learning approaches.

articles.title: La reconnaissance des mots dans la parole accentuée : Une étude en laboratoire et à l’extérieur.
articles.authors: Delphine Deï; Page Elizabeth Piccinini; Isabelle Dautriche; Marieke van Heugten; Alejandrina Cristia; Alex Eguiluz
articles.abstract: Mispronunciations slow down word recognition: A study using touchscreens in the lab and the real world. Recent work suggests that children and adults are initially delayed when exposed to an accented talker, but quickly recover and develop talker-specific listening patterns. This research, however, is often carried out in the lab, where participants’ attention is focused on a single task and no distractions are present, and recovery is often deduced from looking patterns that require little overt response. In this experiment, we overcome these limitations and assess children’s and adults’ word recognition in accented speech, tested in both a laboratory and in a naturalistic setting. We found that mispronunciations in accented speech slow down overt decisions about word recognition, to a similar extent in the lab and in familiar environments, for both children and adults.

articles.title: Facial expression synchrony is associated with neural synchrony during mother-infant interactions
articles.authors: Debora Suppiger; Tilman Reinelt; Sabino Guglielmini; Martin Wolf; Judith M. Burkart; Nathalie Giroud; Moritz M. Daum; Giancarlo Natalucci; Paola Cerrito
articles.abstract: Social interactions depend on the temporal coordination of multiple behavioral and neural processes. This coordination, known as interpersonal synchrony, is thought to support communication and shared understanding, yet how different synchrony modalities relate to one another remains unclear. Here we examined facial expression and neural synchrony during naturalistic play in 86 mother–infant dyads (infant age 7.4 months). Facial expression synchrony was quantified using automated facial action unit coding and windowed cross-lagged correlations, while neural synchrony was assessed using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and wavelet-transform coherence across prefrontal and temporo-parietal regions. Mothers and infants showed strong facial expression synchrony, during approximately 40 % of the interaction and consistent neural synchrony across cortical regions. The two synchrony modalities were related, but associations were localized and bidirectional, suggesting that synchrony across modalities does not arise from a single underlying process. Instead, synchrony may emerge from multiple interacting systems that support flexible social exchange.

articles.title: Cognitive Function and Return to Work: Protocol for a Longitudinal Study Investigating Cognitive Endurance in Stress-Related Disorders
articles.authors: Hanna Malmberg Gavelin; Anastasiya Zakrevska; Magnus Johansson; Anna Nordberg; Elisabeth Björk Brämberg; Fabienne I.M. van Vliet; Birgit H.P.M. Donker-Cools; Frederieke Schaafsma; Anna Finnes
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Patients with long-term stress-related disorders report cognitive symptoms across a broad range of domains; however, neuropsychological test results often do not align with these self-reported cognitive difficulties. One potential explanation for this discrepancy is that patients may perform well during a single, undisturbed test session but have difficulties sustaining cognitive performance over time following prolonged mental effort, which can be conceptualized as reduced cognitive endurance. This may have implications for work participation and hinder return to work unless adequately addressed. 

Methods and analysis: This study protocol describes a longitudinal study aimed at investigating cognitive endurance in patients with long-term stress-related disorders. Moreover, we will explore the association between cognitive endurance and each of the following variables: self-reported fatigue and cognitive function, self-assessed work ability, and return to work. Sixty patients with long-term stress-related disorders will be recruited from a nonrandomized multicentre controlled trial evaluating work-focused cognitive behavioural therapy in a primary healthcare setting. Sixty healthy controls will be recruited through advertisement. Cognitive endurance is assessed through repeated cognitive testing in the morning and afternoon of a regular working day, at two time points: baseline and six months after study enrolment. The cognitive tests focus on short-term and working memory, attention and processing speed, and executive functions. Prior to the assessments, participants complete questionnaires concerning trait fatigue, self-reported cognitive function and work ability. Moreover, state fatigue is assessed through self-report questionnaires administered during the assessment day. Sick-leave registry data is used to investigate return to work for the patient group. The study evaluates a novel method for assessing cognitive functioning in stress-related disorders and can provide insights into how variations in cognitive functioning over the course of a workday relate to different aspects of fatigue, as well as to functioning in everyday life and at work.

Ethics and dissemination: The study has been approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Dnr 2025-01713-01; 2025-07089-02). All participants will receive written and oral information about the study and provide written informed consent. Results will be disseminated in peer-reviewed scientific journals, at academic conferences and through communication with key stakeholders. 

Trial registration: The trial was registered 2 April 2026 at the Open Science Framework (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/CYSGX).

articles.title: Learning Goals and Listening in Polarized Conversations: A Test Across Four Labs
articles.authors: Kenneth G DeMarree; Guy Itzchakov; See Ya Hui Michelle; Netta Weinstein; Taylor Lee; Yaara Turjeman-Levi; Angelia Venezia
articles.abstract: Disagreements often feel threatening, leading people to respond defensively, which can intensify both attitude and social polarization. High-quality listening is a key strategy thought to reduce polarization in these interactions, but this type of listening is rarely employed when disagreeing partners converse, and little is known about how to encourage it. To address this gap, we tested whether conversational goals, specifically, adopting goals to learn about one’s conversational partner versus a goal to persuade one’s conversational partner, can improve high quality listening and, in turn, reduce attitude and social polarization during disagreements. We hypothesized that learning goals foster perceptions of high-quality listening behaviors, which in turn increase partners’ psychological safety, promote open-mindedness, and ultimately reduce polarization. We conducted a large, preregistered experiment across four sites (Israel, Singapore, the U.K., and the U.S.; Total N = 1407). Using live dyadic conversations between strangers who disagreed on a focal topic, we manipulated one participant’s conversational goal and assessed both partners’ experiences. The goal manipulation did not influence perceived listening quality or polarization outcomes in any sample. However, preregistered path analyses provided consistent support across the four labs for the listening-to-depolarization portion of the hypothesized model: Perceived listening quality positively predicted increased psychological safety, which in turn predicted increased open-mindedness and many of the assessed indicators of polarization. The findings highlighted both the need for, and the difficulty of, encouraging high-quality listening during disagreements, with implications for understanding and improving polarization.

articles.title: Word-Level Measures of Syntactic Complexity in Sentence Processing: An Organizing Review
articles.authors: Cas W. Coopmans; Noa Talker-Aharoni; Galit Agmon
articles.abstract: The recent adoption of naturalistic paradigms in the psychology and neuroscience of language has necessitated methods for quantifying incremental syntactic processing complexity. However, there is little consensus about how complexity should be quantified. Existing studies employ a wide range of complexity metrics, reflecting divergent assumptions about the nature of grammatical representations and the mechanisms underlying syntactic processing. Because these assumptions are rarely made explicit, findings across studies cannot be reliably interpreted or consistently synthesized into general conclusions. The goal of the present study is to review the word-level syntactic complexity metrics that have been used to model behavioral and neural measures of syntactic processing. To organize the empirical literature, we introduce a taxonomy based on two complementary dimensions: the grammatical distinction between constituency and dependency representations, and the cognitive distinction between computation- and memory-related aspects of syntactic processing. Our review reveals substantial heterogeneity in how syntactic complexity is operationalized and interpreted, even among ostensibly similar metrics. To test this quantitatively, we applied hierarchical clustering to 26 metrics computed on a sample of 100 annotated sentences. Computation- and memory-related metrics largely clustered together, providing quantitative support for the relevance of our proposed taxonomy. However, this pattern emerged only when constituency- and dependency-based metrics were analyzed separately, showing that the choice of the grammatical formalism shapes how syntactic complexity is quantified. Taken together, these findings underscore the need for greater conceptual clarity in the use of syntactic complexity metrics and for more explicit linking hypotheses connecting linguistic structure to cognitive and neural processes. This review provides a useful framework for achieving these goals.

articles.title: Beyond Behaviour: Autistic Students' Self-Reported Experiences and Expression of Well-Being at School
articles.authors: Annette Carroll; Kate Simpson; Kathryn Ambrose; Dawn Adams
articles.abstract: Autistic students are increasingly represented in mainstream classrooms, yet for many, school remains a source of stress and misunderstanding. While existing research has largely focused on adverse outcomes for autistic students, less attention has been given to identifying indicators of well-being and understanding how it is experienced in everyday school settings. This study addresses this gap by centring autistic students’ perspectives through a flexible, multi‑modal qualitative design. Twelve autistic primary and secondary students shared their experiences through interviews, drawings, written responses, and photovoice methods tailored to their communication preferences and strengths. Data were analysed using inductive content and reflexive thematic analysis. Students described diverse indicators of well‑being across emotional, social, sensory‑physical, and academic domains. High well‑being was often reflected in engagement in learning, access to effective self‑regulation strategies, and expressions of joy, while low well‑being often led to withdrawal, reduced communication, tense posture, and expressions of sadness. Thematic analysis of student experiences highlighted how autistic student well‑being is frequently misunderstood or overlooked. Overall, autistic student well‑being emerged as relational, context‑dependent, and individually patterned, drawing attention to the ways it may be variably expressed, recognised, and responded to in school settings.

articles.title: 90% mental, 10% physical? Psychological and physiological predictors of ultrarunning performance
articles.authors: Annabel de Jong; Allison Matthews; Mark R. Hinder; Nathan Pitchford
articles.abstract: Within the ultrarunning community, performance is often considered ‘90% mental, 10% physical’. This demonstrates the influence of both psychological and physiological factors, particularly emphasising the perceived dominance of psychology. However, extant research typically considers psychological or physiological variables in isolation. Additionally, studies frequently recruit participants from a single ultramarathon, thereby neglecting heterogeneity between events. The current study addresses these limitations by employing an interdisciplinary approach and recruiting participants from a range of races to develop a robust, predictive model of ultrarunning performance. Ultramarathon participants (n = 69 across 24 events) underwent graded exercise testing, psychometric surveys, and physiological/cognitive assessments (Cold Pressor, Stop-Signal, and Serial Sevens tasks). Performance was quantified as percentile finishing time relative to gender-matched event winners. Selection of the initial 15 candidate variables was informed by evidence from relevant literature. A single global model was developed using backwards stepwise regression (Aikake Information Criterion selection), including four covariates: age, gender, apparatus, and distance. The overall model (p < .001, adj. r2 = .426) included VO2max (ß = .609), emotional intelligence (ß = .281), inhibitory control (ß = .259), and sleep behaviours (ß = .226) as key significant predictors. These results demonstrate that the predictability of ultrarunning performance is improved by moving beyond traditional metrics of fitness and considering both psychological and physiological variables. Overall, this model provides an integrated approach for maximising endurance sports training and performance, with broader application to other fields involving physical and psychological exertion (e.g., military, pain management).

articles.title: Scrolling the Nation: Banal Digital Nationalism on Short-Form Video Feeds
articles.authors: Mihai Alexandru Bîclea
articles.abstract: This study inquired into the reproduction of banal digital nationalism on the algorithmically curated short-form video feeds. Rather than emphasizing overt nationalist content, I explored how situated, everyday user–platform interactions reproduce banal forms of nationalist ideology. Through digital diaries and post-hoc semi-structured interviews with Romanian users the analysis was attentive at the entanglement of social, affective and technological structures which habitually reinforce the physical and symbolic borders inherent in nationhood. Algorithmic “re-personalization” and “spacetimemattering” through memes, ads and nostalgic content were identified as forms of routine national (re-)production and normalization on the feed, users becoming oriented towards the nation and their being part of it beyond specific ideational contents. By focusing on an underexplored Eastern European context, the study contributes to research on digital nationalism while demonstrating the utility of new materialist sensibilities for investigating banal digital nationalism.

articles.title: Stable Contexts Are Not Static Causes: A Latent Variable Approach to Time-Varying Consequences of Stable Unobserved Heterogeneity
articles.authors: Baeksan Yu
articles.abstract: Urban-health studies increasingly examine environmental co-occurrences, but longitudinal analyses often rely on fixed-effects (FE) models whose assumptions about stable unobserved heterogeneity are left implicit. This article uses a structural equation modeling (SEM) representation of FE to clarify a narrow but important point: stable, time-invariant, unobserved heterogeneity is controlled by conventional FE only when its contribution to repeated outcomes is also constant across waves. When stable histories of segregation, infrastructure, or governance have changing consequences as environmental co-occurrence configurations are reorganized, conventional FE models may leave residual confounding. I review the classical fixed-effects structural equation modeling (FE-SEM) representation, then present two diagnostic extensions: time-varying-loading FE-SEM (TVL-FE-SEM), a single-latent-dimension model with wave-specific loadings, and constant-and-deviation-loading FE-SEM (CDL-FE-SEM), a two-latent-dimension model that adapts the intercept/slope logic of latent growth modeling to separate common and deviation-loading profiles. A compact Monte Carlo simulation shows that classical FE-SEM recovers the true effect only when stable unobserved heterogeneity enters repeated outcomes with constant loadings, TVL-FE-SEM performs well when the same single latent source has changing loadings, and CDL-FE-SEM helps diagnose whether stable heterogeneity operates through more than one loading profile under a fixed-effects specification, though with finite-sample instability. An empirical illustration using Korean community-health data from 2021–2024 demonstrates the sequence as a diagnostic workflow.

articles.title: Consumer Protection Governance in Gendered Markets: Appearance Pressure, Consumer Awareness, and Gender-Differentiated Pricing in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula Tricity, India
articles.authors: Vishal Thakur
articles.abstract: Gender-differentiated pricing, commonly termed the "Pink Tax," describes situations in which comparable products or services are priced differently by gender. While prior research has documented such price differences, less is known about the behavioral mechanisms shaping how consumers experience them. Drawing on the Political Economy of Beauty and consumer protection governance frameworks, this study examines how appearance pressure, gendered consumption behavior, and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior relate to experienced gender-differentiated pricing among 151 consumers surveyed in the Chandigarh–Mohali–Panchkula tricity, India. Using exploratory factor analysis, correlation, and multiple regression, the results indicate that appearance pressure (β = .407, p < .001) and consumer awareness and price comparison behavior (β = .320, p < .001) significantly predicted experienced gender-differentiated pricing, while gendered consumption behavior did not (β = .128, p = .120), together explaining 44.6% of the variance. These findings suggest that consumers' experiences of differential pricing are shaped more by social expectations around appearance and price awareness than by purchasing behavior alone. Robustness checks (Harman's single-factor test, variance inflation factors, and bootstrapped confidence intervals) support the stability of these results. Given the study's convenience sample and cross-sectional design, findings are presented as exploratory rather than generalizable, with implications framed as hypotheses for future regulatory attention rather than settled policy prescriptions. The study contributes an interdisciplinary behavioral perspective to consumer protection governance research in the Indian context.

articles.title: Dealing with Factor Mismeasurement
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: Empirical implementation of asset pricing models faces a fundamental constraint. The true pricing factors implied by theory are unobservable, so researchers must rely on observable empirical factors. Because these factors are only proxies, they may contain measurement errors that distort estimated factor exposures, risk premia, and assessments of model performance. This study examines factor measurement errors and develops a methodology for assessing their empirical consequences. The methodology allows researchers to evaluate the reliability of asset pricing tests more carefully and draw more credible conclusions from empirical evidence.

articles.title: Shifting toward a Micro ICAPM
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: Intertemporal asset pricing models typically begin with the market factor and introduce additional state variables to capture changes in investment opportunities over time. Empirically, these state variables have traditionally been proxied by macroeconomic variables because they reflect broad shifts in economic conditions affecting the aggregate opportunity set. These proxies are useful at the aggregate level, but less suited to representing variation in investment opportunities across individual assets. This study therefore develops a micro-level approach that replaces macroeconomic proxies with asset-specific variables. The central idea is that a broad set of such variables can more fully represent individual, time-varying investment opportunities.

articles.title: Out of the APT Shadow
articles.authors: Woongki Lee
articles.abstract: In empirical asset pricing, researchers often evaluate a pricing theory through its empirical factor model. This practice is widespread, but rests on a strong premise: the factor model must be a valid empirical proxy for the theory it claims to implement. In most applications, this premise is assumed rather than verified. Good performance alone is not decisive, because a factor model may reflect equilibrium pricing, arbitrage pricing, or both. This study addresses this ambiguity by separating risks arising solely from arbitrage considerations from those relevant to equilibrium pricing. It then tests whether a factor model truly represents equilibrium pricing theory.

articles.title: Operationalizing Qualitative Multimedia Content Analysis for Short-Form Video: A Methods and Data Study of Grooming Precursors Masked as Relationship Advice
articles.authors: Heath Landress
articles.abstract:
Objective: This methods and data article operationalizes qualitative multimedia content analysis (QMCA) for short-form video posts on TikTok and Instagram Reels, focusing on the method's execution and the frequency structure of observable grooming-precursor cues masked as relationship advice.
Method: A purposive corpus of 100 public short-form videos, evenly split between TikTok and Instagram, was archived, de-identified, and coded using MAXQDA 24 for time-segment coding and Excel for the codebook, audit trail, and thresholds. A five-pass routine separated visual features, audio features, on-screen text, and relational/boundary cues. Category development relied on same-document co-occurrence, with recurrence requiring five or more distinct posts.
Results: The final codebook contained 289 codes and produced 1,233 post-level feature hits. Recurrence concentrated in presentation-layer categories: Parasocial Proximity and Platform Normalization appeared in all 100 posts, and Intimate Setting Cues in 80. Covert precursor categories recurred less often: Power Imbalance Normalization in 30 posts, Coercive Reframing in 15, Boundary Erosion in 14, and Isolation and Secrecy in 10.
Conclusions: QMCA provides an auditable method for documenting how short-form advice content packages relational scripts through camera, voice, setting, captioning, and platform conventions. The taxonomy supports prevention-oriented screening without inferring creator intent or labeling any post as grooming.

articles.title: Lessons from Tanzania’s Ujamaa for Smart Settlements in Nepal: Social Justice and Economic Development
articles.authors: Keshav Bhattarai; Ambika P. Adhikari
articles.abstract:
This article examines lessons Nepal can draw from Tanzania’s experience with Ujamaa, the African socialist development model initiated by President Nyerere in 1967. Using comparative policy analysis, published research, official documents, and exploratory field observations from selected Tanzanian locations, including the capital and villages in the Iringa Region, the study evaluates Ujamaa’s achievements and limitations. It assesses their relevance for Nepal’s landless populations and smart-settlement initiatives. The analysis focuses primarily on rural and peri-urban development and does not examine urban squatter housing and rural-to-urban migration.

The comparison demonstrates that some lessons from Tanzania can be considered for Nepal’s own program. Ujamaa contributed to national integration, a shared linguistic identity, literacy, primary education, and rural services. However, it also reduced household autonomy, disrupted existing livelihood systems, and failed to achieve sustained agricultural productivity, employment generation, and income growth. 

The article also briefly discusses Nepal’s own Go to the Village Campaign of 1967, which had mixed success, and Korea’s generally successful 1970 Saemaul Undong movement for a comparative perspective of village-oriented national programs.

The article proposes a Smart Settlement Framework for Nepal based on verified beneficiary identification, differentiated tenure and housing options, voluntary participation, livelihood-oriented site selection, serviced land, cooperative enterprise, accountable local governance, and measurable pathways from social protection to economic mobility.

articles.title: The missing quadrant: perceived voluntariness, option sets and the acceptance of green digital tools
articles.authors: Maha Jehanzeb; Talha Murtaza; Rida Safdar
articles.abstract: Technology acceptance research measures voluntariness as a perception and, in its consumer flagship, assumes it outright, while parallel stream studies explicitly mandate use. It is between the perception and the mandate that a state lies which neither can classify: a use that is formally optional and reported as chosen while the adopter’s set of viable alternatives has been closed off by conditions beyond their control. This paper names that state foreclosed adoption, where the voluntariness assumption of acceptance research is adapted through the lens of the self-determination theory, whose definition of autonomy as endorsement rather than independence entails that the experience of free adoption cannot certify that alternatives existed. The paper goes on to develop a typology of adoption states (volitional, foreclosed, mandated), three foreclosure mechanisms (economic, architectural, relational) with distinct sources and visibilities, an account of leadership style as the mechanism converting foreclosure into internalisation or bare compliance, and eight propositions with an operationalisation agenda. Green digital technology is argued to be the domain where the resulting misclassification costs most, because foreclosed green adoptions are counted twice over, as voluntary and as value driven, inflating estimates of environmental motivation in research and in organisational sustainability metrics.

articles.title: Humanity after the peak: long-run population and human-capital pathways for global environmental change
articles.authors: Samir KC
articles.abstract: Population and human-capital pathways are central to global environmental change research, yet most widely used demographic projections end in 2100. This creates a time-horizon problem for slow-moving environmental processes, including sea-level rise, land-use change, long-lived infrastructure, food-system transformation and adaptation across generations. We extend Shared Socioeconomic Pathways population and human-capital scenarios to 2300 and examine how peak population gives way to long-run demographic decline, aging and regional redistribution. In the middle-of-the-road pathway, the global population declines to about 4.2 billion by 2300. In the sustainability pathway, it approaches 1 billion. These are not extinction scenarios, but they describe a profound change in the social and demographic setting in which environmental demand, exposure, adaptation and policy operate. The results show that the post-2100 period cannot be treated as a simple continuation of twentieth-century population growth. A smaller, older and more educated world may reduce some overall pressures while intensifying others, especially around labor, care, migration and uneven regional change. Long-run environmental analysis, therefore, needs population pathways that extend beyond 2100 and include not only population size, but also age, education, spatial distribution and demographic momentum.

articles.title: Seguros complementarios y gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección de Fonasa: ¿riesgo moral o sesgo de selección? Análisis con microdatos administrativos, Chile, 2022 a 2025
articles.authors: Matias Goyenechea; Alberto Aylwin
articles.abstract:
Introducción. La crisis del sistema de Isapres, la migración de cotizantes hacia el seguro público y la expansión de la oferta de seguros complementarios han modificado los incentivos de gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección de Fonasa. No es claro si el mayor gasto de los beneficiarios asegurados refleja riesgo moral o sesgo de selección.
Objetivos. Estimar, desde la perspectiva del asegurador público, el gasto adicional en la Modalidad de Libre Elección atribuible a la tenencia de un seguro complementario, y descomponerlo en sesgo de selección y riesgo moral, entre 2022 y 2025.
Métodos. Estudio observacional analítico sobre microdatos administrativos individuales (enero 2022 a mayo 2025).El aseguramiento se identificó a partir de su uso efectivo. Se construyó un contrafactual mediante emparejamiento[MG1.1] de vecino más cercano (k = 1, sin reemplazo) sobre covariables observables y se corrigió el error de clasificación con un modelo no lineal de decaimiento por tamaño del hogar. El resultado fue la diferencia porcentual de gasto FAM en la Modalidad de Libre Elección por beneficiario, en unidades reajustables por inflación (unidades de fomento).
Resultados. La brecha bruta de gasto per cápita fue 57,6% mayor en los asegurados; se redujo a 44,2% tras el emparejamiento y convergió a un efecto promedio sobre los tratados de 30,2% (28,8 a 31,3% anual) tras corregir el error de clasificación. 
Conclusiones. El mayor gasto asociado a seguros complementarios combina selección de riesgo y riesgo moral; al menos unos 13 puntos porcentuales corresponden a diferencias de composición de la población que contrata seguros complementarios. Los seguros complementarios se asocian a un aumento del gasto en la Modalidad de Libre Elección del orden de 30% una vez controlados los sesgos observables y de clasificación.

articles.title: Social spending and democratic institutions in Southeast Asia: A comparative study between Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines
articles.authors: FADILLAH PUTRA
articles.abstract:
Purpose
This paper aims to analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries. Furthermore, this essay will also challenge the theory that the government system (majoritarian versus consensus democracy) influences the magnitude of social spending and welfare commitment, especially in Southeast Asian democracies, namely, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines.

Design/methodology/approach
This research uses descriptive statistics and qualitative data to match social spending with the development of democratisation in four cases.

Findings
The main argument is whether the presence of democratic institutions encourages the government to be more open, citizen-oriented and responsive or whether the inclusive political conditions will create more open public participation in the policymaking process. Thus, in the context of developing countries, public participation will be more likely to demand social policies.

Research limitations/implications
It has not been able to undertake a more detailed impact evaluation assessment of the development and change of democratic institutions towards policy outcomes within a shorter temporal scope. In addition, this thesis does not also provide details or explanations about the interaction process between particular democratic institutions and specific social policy sectors.

Practical implications
The process of interactions between particular electoral systems. For instance, the contribution to the emergence of policy in the health services sector or conducting research in normative democratic institutions such as public awareness of the importance of public participation in shaping and directing the implementation of poverty reduction policies could be studied, by using the historical institutionalism approach.

Originality/value
The impact of certain political institutions on public policy has become a very important discussion in the new institutionalism perspective. Social policy (social spending) as a manifestation of government’s commitment towards welfare is the result of institutional arrangement. In the context of developing countries, where social policy is needed to fulfill the basic needs of citizens, it is important to identify what kind of institutional formations are conducive to the development of social policy. This essay will analyse how democratic institutions affects social spending formations in the context of developing countries.

articles.title: The Harder the State Hits: Coercive Intensity, Protest Repression, and Terrorist Backlash
articles.authors: Ana Cristancho
articles.abstract:
Why does repression sometimes deter dissent but at other times generate terrorist backlash? Existing theories emphasise political opportunity, grievances, legitimacy and strategic interaction, but they do not fully explain when repression against dissent escalates into terrorist violence. I argue that backlash depends on the coercive mode through which state force is organised and interpreted. Coercion is more likely to deter when it remains proportionate, fair and predictable. Backlash becomes more likely when coercion creates two interconnected expectation gaps. The first is instrumental: compliance no longer appears sufficient to guarantee safety. The second is normative: the state violates its own claim to exercise force within bounded limits, signalling the exclusion of some groups rather than their protection. Under these conditions, excessive, arbitrary, indiscriminate or visibly disproportionate coercion weakens deterrence while intensifying grievance. It changes the moral ecology through which dissent is interpreted, making terrorist retaliation appear more strategically plausible or morally defensible.

I test this argument using country-quarter event data from ACLED and GTD for 2018–2021. The results show that coercive military involvement in domestic security is associated with higher subsequent terrorist activity. The association follows a coercion-intensity gradient: excessive force and military protest repression are more strongly associated with subsequent terrorism than lower-intensity intervention or police-led repression. These findings hold across alternative controls, temporal diagnostics and balancing checks, but remain observational. They suggest that repression backfires not simply because it is forceful, but because some forms of coercion undermine the legitimacy and predictability on which deterrence depends.

articles.title: A Rejoinder to 'Still Instrumentally Inclusive' (Turnbull-Dugarte & López Ortega)
articles.authors: Daniel de Kadt
articles.abstract: Turnbull-Dugarte and López Ortega's "Still Instrumentally Inclusive" (the Response) answers my replication (the Comment) of their 2024 American Political Science Review paper (the Article) with, among other things, a multiverse of 2,970 analyses based on eighteen different weighting schemes, randomization inference, and a trichotomous moderator. As I show in this rejoinder, each is undermined by bona fide errors in their code, their writing, and their interpretation. First, the multiverse is just many correlated variants of the same test. This is in large part due to the weighting schemes which suffer multiple problems (some due to code errors, some intrinsic), and are largely correlated variations on one weighting scheme. Second, due to code errors the randomization inference compares a weighted statistic against an unweighted null and, in the two heterogeneity tests, permutes the interaction column rather than treatment assignment column. Every permutation p-value the Response reports is therefore computed against the wrong reference distribution; when they are recomputed correctly, two of the five it reports as significant are no longer so, and they are the two the Response emphasizes. Third, the trichotomous moderator is erroneously described as terciles, but it is in fact based on non-tercile cutpoints. The key subgroup effect reported in the Response thus rests on comparing just thirty high-weight control respondents against thirty-one high-weight treated respondents, and ends up reaffirming my original point that the heterogeneity in study 2 is with respect to weights, and not immigration sentiment as their theory predicts. I close by documenting seven claims in the Response that are untrue or misleading.

articles.title: THE FORMATION OF THE U.S. HEGEMONIC REVOLUTIONARY BLOC
articles.authors: Aleksandar Korolija
